Chapter 3 Constitutive equations

3.6 Work and strain energy

In section 3.5 we computed how much work a machine does when it stretches a steel bar slowly. The force at the end of the bar grows from zero to 10 kN, the end of the bar moves by 6,496 mm, and the work is 32,48 J. Now we ask where this work goes. When we unload the bar slowly, it shortens back to its original length and pulls the machine along as it does so. Does it give back all the work it received? And what about a small piece of material inside a body, where not only the stretch in one direction changes, but all the strain components at once?

The section sets out to answer three questions. First, how much work it takes to deform a small piece of material, and where that work goes. Second, what it means that a material stores the work and gives all of it back on unloading, and what follows from this for the elastic constants. We will show that the material stiffness matrix of such a material is symmetric, which keeps the promise of section 3.4 that there are at most 21 different constants, and that the bulk modulus and the shear modulus of an isotropic material must be positive if the material is to be stable, that is, if it is not to deform by itself, without a force. Third, how the stored energy splits into a part that changes the volume of the piece and a part that changes its shape. At the end we meet an energy in which stress and strain swap roles, which we will need in chapter 4.

The physical model is this. We load the body slowly. This means two things: the body is in equilibrium at every instant, and all its parts move so slowly that their kinetic energy is negligible compared with the work of the forces. We call such loading quasi-static loading (kvazistatično obremenjevanje) (the assumption SADD §6.1, PDF p. 128, the term BOWER §1.1.4, PDF p. 34). In the first subsection we show with numbers what slowly means: the settling time is very short compared with the loading time. The strains are small, all components at most \(0{,}001\) in absolute value as before, so we compute with the small strain tensor (definition 1.121) and with areas and volumes before loading. The temperature does not change, so there are no strains caused by temperature as in section 3.3. At first we assume nothing about the material. Then, step by step, we assume that it gives the work back, that it is linear elastic (definition 3.9) and that it is isotropic (definition 3.10). For every claim we say which of these assumptions it uses.

The route is this. First we look at where the work goes in the bar, and we convert it to a unit of volume. Then we write the same account for every instant and for a whole body, from the top, with the law of conservation of energy. After that we go from the bottom and compute the work that the surrounding material does on a small box when all its strain components change. From the requirement that the material gives back all the work along any loading path, we obtain an energy per unit volume that depends only on the strain, and we show that the stresses are its partial derivatives. From this it follows that an elastic constant does not change when the first and the second pair of indices are swapped, and which bounds the constants must satisfy.

3.6.1 Where the work goes

Recall the setting of section 3.5 (figure 3.101). The steel bar of chapter 2 has length \(L = 10\) m and a round cross section of diameter 10 mm, with area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\). The left end is held by the fixed jaw of a tension testing machine, and the machine pulls the right end along the axis of the bar with a force that it raises slowly from zero to \(F_1 = 10\) kN. We neglect the weight of the bar, because it is only 0,6 % of the final force (section 3.5). The elongation by which the right end has moved up to a given instant is called \(e\), and we draw the stretched bar in orange. The stress stays below the yield stress of 220 MPa throughout, so the force is proportional to the elongation, \(F(e) = k\,e\). The number \(k = EA/L = 1{,}539 \cdot 10^6\) N/m says how much force each metre of elongation takes, and \(E = 196\) GPa is Young's modulus of steel (definition 3.1). At the final force the elongation is \(\Delta L = F_1/k = 6{,}496\) mm. The function \(\tfrac12 k\,e^2\) has the derivative \(k\,e\), so by the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.55, item 1, the work the force does on the way from \(e = 0\) to \(e = \Delta L\) is

\[\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\Delta L} k\,e\,\mathrm{d}e &= \tfrac12\,k\,\Delta L^2 = \tfrac12\,F_1\,\Delta L \\ &= \tfrac12 \cdot 10\,000\ \text{N} \cdot 6{,}496 \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 32{,}48\ \text{J} . \end{aligned} \tag{3.57}\]

In the second step we used \(k\,\Delta L = F_1\). On the graph of force \(F\) against elongation \(e\) this work is the area of the triangle under the line from the origin \(O\) to the force \(F_1\) and the elongation \(\Delta L\), and \(32{,}48\) J is written into the triangle (figure 3.126, left).

Why did we pull the bar slowly? When the end of the bar moves, the material of the bar moves too, and part of the work could go into motion. Let us estimate how much. Pulled slowly, the bar stretches evenly, each of its parts by the same fraction of its length. This is an assumption. It holds when the axial force is nearly the same in all cross sections, and in the next subsection we compute that in our pulling it differs along the bar by only \(2 \cdot 10^{-5}\) of its value. It does not hold in a jerk, when the end already moves while the material at the jaw is still at rest. The point that was at distance \(x\) from the jaw before loading therefore moves by \(e\,x/L\) when the end moves by \(e\): by nothing at \(x = 0\), by the whole \(e\) at \(x = L\). Suppose the machine pulls the end of the bar with the force \(F\) and moves it at a constant speed \(v\), so that the elongation grows by \(v\,\Delta t\) in the time \(\Delta t\). The displacement of the point at \(x\) then grows by \(v\,\Delta t\,x/L\), so its speed is \(v\,x/L\) (figure 3.124). The piece of the bar between \(x\) and \(x + \Delta x\) has the mass \(\rho A\,\Delta x\), where \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³ is the density of steel, and the kinetic energy \(\tfrac12\,\rho A\,\Delta x\,(v x/L)^2\), half the mass times the square of the speed (EP §3.1.2, p. 102). We get the kinetic energy of the whole bar by adding up the contributions of the pieces and making the pieces shorter, that is, with an integral. The function \(x^3/3\) has the derivative \(x^2\), so by the fundamental theorem of calculus the kinetic energy of the bar is

\[\int_0^L \tfrac12\,\rho A\,\frac{v^2 x^2}{L^2}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{\rho A\,v^2}{2L^2} \cdot \frac{L^3}{3} = \frac{m\,v^2}{6} ,\]

where \(m = \rho A L = 6{,}126\) kg is the mass of the bar. Where does the six come from? The half comes from the formula for kinetic energy. The third says that the points of the bar do not all move with the speed \(v\). The speed grows from zero at the jaw to \(v\) at the end, its square grows along a parabola from zero to \(v^2\), and the average of this parabola over the length of the bar is a third of its largest value, as the integral \(\int_0^L x^2\,\mathrm{d}x = L^3/3\) says.

If the machine stretched the bar in a single second, the speed of the end would be \(v = 6{,}496\) mm/s, and the kinetic energy of the bar at the end of the stretching would be

\[\frac{m\,v^2}{6} = \frac{6{,}126\ \text{kg} \cdot (6{,}496 \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{m/s})^2}{6} = 4{,}3 \cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{J} ,\]

which is \(1{,}3 \cdot 10^{-6}\) of the work of 32,48 J, about a millionth. With slower stretching it is smaller still, because it grows with the square of the speed. Almost all the work of the machine therefore goes into the material of the bar. This is what slowly means: the kinetic energy is negligible compared with the work. The sources, too, assume in their derivations of energy that the stress grows so slowly that inertia does not count (SADD §6.1, PDF p. 128, EP §3.1.2, p. 100). BOWER also gives a criterion for when loading is slow enough (BOWER §1.1.4, PDF p. 34). For the estimate he takes the speed of a shear wave (strižno valovanje), that is, of a shear disturbance travelling through the solid. In steel this speed is

\[c = \sqrt{\frac{G}{\rho}} = \sqrt{\frac{75{,}38 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa}}{7800\ \text{kg/m}^3}} = 3109\ \text{m/s} ,\]

where \(G\) is the shear modulus of steel (definition 3.17). In figure 3.125 we draw the disturbance as a blue line that runs along the bar from the jaw towards the end. The stresses settle to the values they would have at rest in about ten times the time the disturbance needs to cross the body, here the length \(L\). If the load does not change noticeably in that time, a computation as if the body were in equilibrium is enough. For our bar this time is \(10\,L/c = 100\ \text{m}/(3109\ \text{m/s}) = 0{,}032\) s, more than thirty times shorter than one second, the duration of the loading. On the time axis, drawn to scale, it is only a short piece at the start. A disturbance that stretches or shortens the bar along its axis travels faster, at the speed \(\sqrt{E/\rho} = 5013\) m/s (GR §7.5.3, PDF p. 580), and crosses the bar ten times in only \(0{,}020\) s. The estimate with the speed of the shear wave is therefore on the safe side.

Where does the work go? We now unload the bar slowly. Below the yield stress it returns along the same line along which it was loaded (figure 2.18, grey arrow, and figure 3.126, left, the grey double arrow). Who does the work is told by the direction of the force and the direction of the motion, so let us draw both (figure 3.127). The bar is held on the left by the jaw and at its right end by the machine's grip, which has already moved the end by the elongation \(e\) from its place before loading. During loading (top) the grip pulls the end of the bar with the force \(k\,e\) to the right and also moves to the right. Force and motion point the same way, so the bar receives work. During unloading (bottom) the grip moves back towards the jaw. The bar is still stretched, so the grip still pulls it to the right, and by the law of action and reaction the bar pulls the grip towards itself with the equal force \(k\,e\) to the left. The force of the bar and the motion of the grip point the same way, so now the bar does work on the machine. Since the force at every elongation is the same as during loading, this work is again the area of the same triangle, 32,48 J. The bar has stored the work and given all of it back, like a spring. The energy that a body stores because it is deformed is called strain energy (deformacijska energija) (SADD §6.1, PDF p. 128, BOWER §3.2.7, PDF p. 102). We write it \(U\). For our bar \(U = 32{,}48\) J.

Above the yield stress it is different. If we stretch the bar from the origin \(O\) up to the point \(B\) in figure 2.18 and then unload it, it returns along a line parallel to the initial one and stays permanently longer at zero force. The area under the loading curve is the work the machine did, the area under the unloading line the work the bar gave back (figure 3.126, right, on the axes \(\varepsilon\) and \(\sigma\)). The difference, the grey area between the curve and the line, is not given back. The first law of thermodynamics says where it goes: the work done by the stresses is either stored in the material as energy that the material can give back, or turned into heat, or both (BOWER §3.1.1, PDF p. 93). Some materials turn part of the work into heat even below the yield stress, and under repeated loading their loading and unloading curves form a loop. BOWER describes such materials with the viscoelastic model, which we mentioned in section 3.1.9 and in which the stress also depends on how fast the strain changes (BOWER §1.1.5, PDF p. 35). For metals below the yield stress we neglect this part, as is usual with the linear elastic model (BOWER §1.1.5, PDF p. 34).

How much energy does one cubic metre of steel in our bar store? All parts of the bar are stretched equally and equally stressed, so every cubic centimetre of the bar stores an equal share of the energy. The volume of the bar is \(V = A L = 78{,}540 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2 \cdot 10\ \text{m} = 7{,}8540 \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^3\), and the energy per unit volume is \(32{,}481\ \text{J}/(7{,}8540 \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^3) = 41\,356\ \text{J/m}^3\). In figure 3.126, left, we read it from the same triangle. We divide the force on the vertical axis by the area \(A\) and the elongation on the horizontal one by the length \(L\), which gives the grey axes \(\sigma\) and \(\varepsilon\). The shape stays the same, its area is divided by \(A L\) and is now \(41\,356\ \text{J/m}^3\). Let us write it with the stress and the strain of the bar:

\[\frac{U}{A L} = \frac{\tfrac12\,F_1\,\Delta L}{A L} = \frac12 \cdot \frac{F_1}{A} \cdot \frac{\Delta L}{L} = \tfrac12\,\sigma\,\varepsilon ,\]

where \(\sigma = F_1/A = 127{,}324\) MPa is the stress in the bar (definition 2.6) and \(\varepsilon = \Delta L/L = \sigma/E\) its strain (definition 1.2). Indeed \(\tfrac12\,\sigma\,\varepsilon = \sigma^2/(2E) = (127{,}324 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa})^2/(2 \cdot 196 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa}) = 41\,356\ \text{J/m}^3\). The units agree, because \(1\ \text{Pa} = 1\ \text{N/m}^2 = 1\ \text{N}\,\text{m}/\text{m}^3 = 1\ \text{J/m}^3\). The half has the same origin as for the work: during loading the stress grew evenly from zero to \(\sigma\), so on average it was \(\sigma/2\), and the triangle is half of the rectangle with the sides \(\sigma\) and \(\varepsilon\).

The expression \(\tfrac12\,\sigma\,\varepsilon\) no longer contains the length and the cross-section area of the bar, only the stress and the strain of the material. The energy per unit volume is therefore a property of the state of the material, not of the bar. In the bar, however, only the stress along the axis was nonzero, and the relation between stress and strain was a straight line. What about a small piece of material in a body, where all the stress and strain components change, and a material for which the relation is not a straight line? To answer, we must compute how much work the forces on the faces of a small piece do.

3.6.2 The energy account of a whole body

For the bar we compared the work of the machine and the stored energy at the end of loading. Now we write the same account for every instant, and from the top: we start from the whole body and the law of conservation of energy and descend to what happens in the material. In the next subsection we go from the bottom, from the forces on the faces of a small box, and arrive at the same expression. The view from the top says what this expression is for: it is the part of the power of the external forces that does not go into motion. The view from the bottom says why exactly these components of stress and strain appear in it.

Take any body and look at what supplies energy to it in a short time (figure 3.128). Work done per unit time is called power (moč), its unit is the watt, \(1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J/s}\). A force whose point of action moves does in a short time the work equal to the component of the force in the direction of motion times the path, so its power is the component of the force in the direction of the velocity times the speed.

  1. The surroundings act on the surface of the body with surface forces, with the traction vector \(\vek t\) per unit area (definition 2.20). Under them the surface moves with the velocity \(\vek v\). We denote the power of all the surface forces together by \(P_{\mathrm{A}}\).
  2. On every small piece inside acts the body force \(\vek b\) per unit volume, for example the weight (definition 2.28). The piece moves too. The power of all the body forces is \(P_{\mathrm{V}}\).
  3. The body can also receive heat from the surroundings, \(Q\) joules per second.
  4. The body has two stores of energy. The first is the energy of motion \(T\), the sum of the contributions \(\tfrac12 m v^2\) of all its pieces, which we computed for the bar above. The second is the internal energy \(U\) (notranja energija), everything that is stored in the material itself: the energy the material has because it is deformed, and the energy of the thermal motion of its molecules (CM §5.4.2, PDF p. 236).

The first law of thermodynamics says that energy is neither lost nor created: what flows into the body collects in the stores,

\[\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,(T + U) = P_{\mathrm{A}} + P_{\mathrm{V}} + Q \tag{3.58}\]

(CM (5.4.1), PDF p. 236). On the left is the rate at which the stores grow, on the right the three flows. The equation is a law of nature, found by measurement, and we do not derive it.

In this section we leave out the heat, \(Q = 0\). This is an assumption. Why it is justified here: by the assumption at the start of the section the temperature of the body does not change, and below the yield stress the work of the stresses does not turn into heat, as we saw for the bar, which gave back all the work. When it does not hold: above the yield stress, where the work that is not given back in figure 3.126 becomes heat, for viscoelastic materials and for bodies that are heated. The flow of heat through a body and the stresses it causes are treated in chapter 14. What the assumption does to the result: without \(Q\) all the power of the forces that does not go into motion is stored as energy of deformation, and \(U\) is then the strain energy of the previous subsection.

How much of the power goes into motion and how much into the material? We show it on a bar, where an integral along the length is enough for the whole account, and then say what changes for a body.

The setting is this (figure 3.129). The bar lies along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\), where \(x\) means the position of a cross-section before loading. Before loading the cross-section has the area \(A\) and the material the density \(\rho\). The displacement of the cross-section \(x\) at the time \(t\) is \(u(x, t)\), its velocity \(v = \partial u/\partial t\), its acceleration \(a = \partial v/\partial t\), and the strain of the bar is \(\varepsilon = \partial u/\partial x\) (definition 1.2). The axial force in a cross-section is \(N(x, t) = \sigma A\) (definition 2.5). The surroundings pull the right end with the force \(N(L, t)\) along the axis and the left end with the force \(N(0, t)\) in the opposite direction, both arrows are drawn for tension. Along the bar acts also a distributed force \(q\) per unit length in the direction of the axis, for the hanging bar the weight \(\rho g A\). The blue arrows are the velocities of five cross-sections. We assume that \(u\) is twice continuously differentiable in \(x\) and \(t\) and \(N\) continuously differentiable in \(x\), so that we may use the theorems below, and that \(Q = 0\).

  1. The power of the external forces. The force at the right end has the power \(N(L, t)\,v(L, t)\), the force at the left end \(-N(0, t)\,v(0, t)\), because it points against the axis. A piece of length \(h\) carries the force \(q\,h\) and moves with the velocity \(v\), its contribution is \(q\,v\,h\). The sum over the pieces is a Riemann sum, so
    \[P = N(L, t)\,v(L, t) - N(0, t)\,v(0, t) + \int_0^L q\,v\,\mathrm{d}x .\]
  2. We carry the end forces into the interior. Integration by parts (corollary 3.56) with \(f = N\) and \(g = v\) as functions of the position \(x\) at a chosen time gives
    \[N(L, t)\,v(L, t) - N(0, t)\,v(0, t) = \int_0^L \frac{\partial N}{\partial x}\,v\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_0^L N\,\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}x .\]
    In figure 3.123 the left side is the large rectangle without the small one, the right side both shapes along the curve.
  3. We insert this into step 1 and by the linearity of the integral (lemma 3.54, item 1) join the two terms with the velocity:
    \[P = \int_0^L \Big(\frac{\partial N}{\partial x} + q\Big)\,v\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_0^L N\,\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}x .\]
  4. Newton's law for a piece. We cut out the piece between \(x\) and \(x + h\) as a free body. The right part of the bar pulls it with the force \(N(x + h, t)\), the left part with the force \(N(x, t)\) in the opposite direction, and \(q\,h\) acts on it as well. Its mass is \(\rho A h\). We compute it with the density, the area and the length before loading, because the piece contains the same matter all the time: when it stretches and gets thinner, its mass does not change. This is conservation of mass, and because of it we may integrate over the positions \(x\) before loading. The resultant of the forces is the mass times the acceleration \(a\) (section 2.7.8, the paragraph on a body that moves):
    \[N(x + h, t) - N(x, t) + q\,h \approx \rho A h\,a(x, t) .\]
    The sign \(\approx\) stands because \(q\) and \(a\) change a little along the piece. We divide by \(h\). As \(h\) goes to zero, the left side is by the definition of the partial derivative 1.26 equal to \(\partial N/\partial x + q\), and the error goes to zero, because \(q\) and \(a\) are continuous:
    \[\frac{\partial N}{\partial x} + q = \rho A\,a . \tag{3.59}\]
    For a bar at rest \(a = 0\), and the equation says that the axial force falls as fast as the distributed force replaces it.
  5. The difference of velocities is the rate of stretching. By theorem 1.131 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives
    \[\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial t} .\]
    If two neighbouring cross-sections move equally fast, the piece between them only moves along. It starts to stretch when the right one is faster than the left one, as with the arrows that grow to the right.
  6. We insert steps 4 and 5 into step 3:
    \[P = \int_0^L \rho A\,a\,v\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_0^L N\,\frac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial t}\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{3.60}\]
  7. The first integral is the power that goes into motion. A piece of mass \(\rho A h\) has the energy of motion \(\tfrac12\,\rho A h\,v^2\). By the product rule (lemma 1.82, item 3) the derivative of \(v^2 = v \cdot v\) with respect to time is \(2\,v\,a\), so the energy of motion of the piece grows at the rate \(\rho A h\,a\,v\). The sum over the pieces is the first integral, so it is \(\mathrm{d}T/\mathrm{d}t\). That the derivative with respect to time may be exchanged with the integral over \(x\) is shown in chapter 4, and here we check the equality on the numbers below.
  8. What remains goes into the material. There are only two stores, \(T\) and \(U\). By the first law (3.58) with \(Q = 0\) and \(P_{\mathrm{A}} + P_{\mathrm{V}} = P\) we have \(\mathrm{d}T/\mathrm{d}t + \mathrm{d}U/\mathrm{d}t = P\). We subtract step 7 and get
    \[\frac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}t} = \int_0^L N\,\frac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial t}\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L \sigma\,\frac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial t}\,A\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{3.61}\]

The internal energy of the bar thus grows at a rate set only by the stress and the strain rate in its cross-sections. The external forces are no longer in the result: integration by parts carried the end forces into the interior, and the part with the derivative of the axial force became, together with \(q\) and by Newton's law, the power that goes into motion.

Let us check the steps on the bar of the previous subsection, with \(L = 10\) m, the mass \(m = \rho A L = 6{,}126\) kg and no distributed force, \(q = 0\). Let the machine pull the end with the speed \(v_{\mathrm{e}} = 6{,}496\) mm/s, which it reached in a tenth of a second, so that the acceleration of the end is \(a_{\mathrm{e}} = 0{,}06496\ \text{m/s}^2\), and let the force at the end be \(F = 10\) kN at this instant. We assume that the bar stretches uniformly, the velocity of a cross-section is \(v_{\mathrm{e}}\,x/L\) and its acceleration \(a_{\mathrm{e}}\,x/L\), as in figure 3.124. Then \(\partial\varepsilon/\partial t = v_{\mathrm{e}}/L\) in all cross-sections.

quantity expression value
power of the machine \(P\) \(F\,v_{\mathrm{e}}\) \(64{,}96\) W
power that goes into motion \(\int_0^L \rho A\,\dfrac{a_{\mathrm{e}} x}{L}\,\dfrac{v_{\mathrm{e}} x}{L}\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{m\,a_{\mathrm{e}} v_{\mathrm{e}}}{3}\) \(8{,}617 \cdot 10^{-4}\) W
axial force from (3.59) \(N(x) = F - \rho A\,a_{\mathrm{e}}\,\dfrac{L^2 - x^2}{2L}\) \(N(0) = F - 0{,}199\) N
power that goes into the material \(\int_0^L N\,\dfrac{v_{\mathrm{e}}}{L}\,\mathrm{d}x = F\,v_{\mathrm{e}} - \dfrac{m\,a_{\mathrm{e}} v_{\mathrm{e}}}{3}\) \(64{,}96\) W less \(8{,}617 \cdot 10^{-4}\) W

The second row is the derivative with respect to time of the energy of motion \(m v_{\mathrm{e}}^2/6\) of the previous subsection, \(m\,v_{\mathrm{e}} a_{\mathrm{e}}/3\), which confirms step 7. The third row solves equation (3.59) with \(N(L) = F\): the axial force at the grip is smaller by \(0{,}199\) N than at the end, because the difference has to accelerate the bar, whose cross-sections move faster and faster towards the end. The sum of the second and the fourth row is the first (checked with SymPy). Of the power of the machine \(1{,}3 \cdot 10^{-5}\) goes into motion, everything else into the material. The assumption of uniform stretching is thereby justified to the same accuracy: the axial force, and with it the strain, differs along the bar by \(2 \cdot 10^{-5}\) of its value. For slow loading therefore \(\mathrm{d}U/\mathrm{d}t = F\,v_{\mathrm{e}}\), and when we add this up over time, we get the work \(\int_0^{\Delta L} k\,e\,\mathrm{d}e = 32{,}48\) J of equation (3.57).

From the whole bar to a point. Steps 1 to 8 can be repeated for any part of the bar between the cross-sections \(x_1 < x_2\). The external forces are then the axial forces \(N(x_1, t)\) and \(N(x_2, t)\) with which the neighbouring parts act on it, as on the cut-out piece, and we get the same equation with the limits \(x_1\) and \(x_2\). Let \(w(x, t)\) be the energy stored per unit volume, so that a part of the bar has the internal energy \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} w\,A\,\mathrm{d}x\). Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} \Big(\frac{\partial w}{\partial t} - \sigma\,\frac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial t}\Big)\,A\,\mathrm{d}x = 0 \qquad \text{for every pair } x_1 < x_2 .\]

A continuous function whose integral over every interval is zero is zero everywhere. If it were positive in some cross-section, by continuity it would be positive on a short interval around it, and the integral over that interval would be positive. So in every cross-section

\[\frac{\partial w}{\partial t} = \sigma\,\frac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial t} . \tag{3.62}\]

The right side is called the stress power (moč napetosti) per unit volume (CM (5.4.11), PDF p. 238). The equation holds at a point, and that is why it mattered that the account holds for every part of the bar, not only for the whole.

May we conclude from (3.62) that \(w = \sigma\,\varepsilon\)? No. The stored energy is the sum over time of the contributions \(\sigma\,\partial\varepsilon/\partial t\), and the stress changes during loading. The product \(\sigma\,\varepsilon\) of the final values would be right only if the stress had its final value all the time. In figure 3.126 this is the rectangle with the sides \(\sigma\) and \(\varepsilon\), \(82\,712\ \text{J/m}^3\), while the true energy is the triangle under the line, \(41\,356\ \text{J/m}^3\). The half holds only for a line, that is for a linear elastic material. For a curve the energy is the area under it and is neither \(\sigma\,\varepsilon\) nor \(\tfrac12\,\sigma\,\varepsilon\).

A body instead of a bar. For a body the steps are the same, only the tools are spatial. The integral over a body and the divergence theorem come in chapter 4 (theorem 4.14), so here we only list the steps beside figure 3.128, where the surface forces and the body forces are drawn, and state the result (BOWER §2.4.1 and §2.4.3, PDF pp. 81-84, CM (5.4.7)-(5.4.11), PDF pp. 237-238).

step bar body
power of the external forces the end forces and \(q\) surface forces over the whole surface, body forces over the whole volume
carrying into the interior integration by parts Cauchy's formula \(\vek t = \ten\sigma\,\vek n\) and the divergence theorem
Newton's law \(\partial N/\partial x + q = \rho A\,a\) the equations of motion of section 2.7.8, with \(\rho\,a_{\mathrm{i}}\) on the right
what remains \(N\,\partial\varepsilon/\partial t\) the sum of the products of \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and the derivatives of the velocity \(\partial v_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\)

In rotation the small square only turns, the angle between its sides stays right. The shear stresses \(\tau\) on it form two pairs, one on the horizontal and one on the vertical sides. In rotation the horizontal sides move along their pair, the vertical ones against theirs, so the work of one pair is positive, of the other negative, and the sum is zero. In shear the angle between the sides changes, the stresses do positive work and nothing cancels it.

Only one thing is new. The derivative of the velocity with respect to position is the time derivative of the displacement gradient, and the displacement gradient is the sum of the small strain tensor and the small rotation tensor (definition 1.122). In a bar there is no rotation. In a body a small piece can also turn while it moves, and we must ask whether the stresses do work in that. They do not: the stress matrix is symmetric, the rate of rotation antisymmetric, and the sum of the products of the elements in the same places of such a pair is zero (lemma 1.107 on the double-dot product of a symmetric and an antisymmetric matrix). In the next subsection we see the same in a figure: in a rotation one pair of shear forces does as much positive work as the other does negative. What remains is

\[\frac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}t} = \int_{\mathcal \mathrm{B}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial t}\,\mathrm{d}V , \qquad \frac{\partial w}{\partial t} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}}{\partial t} . \tag{3.63}\]
\[\dot U = \int_{\mathcal \mathrm{B}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\dot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V , \qquad \dot w = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\dot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} . \tag{3.63}\]

Here \(\mathcal B\) is the region the body occupies, the indices \(i\) and \(j\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), and the second equation follows from the first because the first holds for every part of the body, as for the bar. In the bar only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma\) differs from zero, and the equations become (3.61) and (3.62).

We integrated over the shape of the body before loading, with the areas and volumes as they were then. This is the assumption of small displacements. Why it is justified here: for strains up to \(0{,}001\) the volume of a small piece changes by at most \(0{,}3\) per cent, in our bar by \((1 - 2\nu)\,\varepsilon = 0{,}4 \cdot 6{,}496 \cdot 10^{-4} = 0{,}026\) per cent, and the energy per unit volume is wrong by as much. When it does not hold: the rubber band of section 2.13.1 stretches by a half and its cross-section shrinks by a third. There one has to say which area and volume are meant, and the stress power takes another form, which we write in section @sec-hiperelasticni.

In the lectures the energy of motion is denoted by \(K\) and called kinetic energy, the power of the external forces by \(P\), the body force by \(\vek f\), and the time derivative by a dot. The internal energy is written there per unit mass, with the small letter \(u\), which for us means the displacement. Our energy per unit volume is \(w = \rho\,u\).

3.6.3 The work of the stresses on a small box

Take any body that we load slowly, and a point \(P\) in its interior. At \(P\) we imagine a small box with edges \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta y\) and \(\Delta z\) parallel to the axes of a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, and with volume \(\Delta V = \Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z\) (figure 3.133). The material around the box acts on it with forces on its six faces. Let us follow a short stage of the loading, during which the displacement of every point \(Q\) of the box changes by a small vector \(\Delta\vek u(Q)\). How much work do the forces on the faces do?

We also need the rule for the work when the force does not necessarily point in the direction of the motion (figure 3.131). When the point on which a constant force \(\vek F\) acts moves along a short segment \(\Delta\vek u\), the force does the work \(\vek F\cdot\Delta\vek u\), the scalar product of the force and the displacement (EP (3.1.1), p. 97). This is the length of the displacement times the component of the force in the direction of the displacement (definition 2.13). When the force points in the direction of the displacement, this is the school rule, force times distance. When the force is perpendicular to the displacement, the work is zero. When it points against the displacement, the work is negative. We will deal more carefully with work for displacements in any direction in chapter 4.

We simplify the computation with two assumptions, which hold approximately for a small box (figure 3.132). First, the stress is the same at all points of the box and does not change noticeably during the short stage. Second, the change of displacement is a linear function of position, which differs from the true change only by a small remainder: for every point \(Q\) of the box and for \(i = x, y, z\),

\[\begin{aligned} \Delta u_{\mathrm{i}}(Q) &= \Delta u_{\mathrm{i}}(P) + \Delta H_{\mathrm{ix}}\,(x_{\mathrm{Q}} - x_{\mathrm{P}}) \\ &\quad + \Delta H_{\mathrm{iy}}\,(y_{\mathrm{Q}} - y_{\mathrm{P}}) + \Delta H_{\mathrm{iz}}\,(z_{\mathrm{Q}} - z_{\mathrm{P}}) , \end{aligned} \tag{3.64}\]

where \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is the change during the stage of the partial derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) at the point \(P\), that is, the change of the entry of the displacement gradient in row \(i\) and column \(j\) (definition 1.112). Here \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) stands for the coordinate \(x\), \(y\) or \(z\). By theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step, the true change of displacement differs from this one by a remainder that is small compared with the size of the box. An exact computation also takes into account that the stress varies a little across the box, and the weight of the box. The weight does work when the box moves, but the difference of the forces on opposite faces, which balances the weight, does exactly as much work with the opposite sign (section 2.7). The other terms left out are smaller by a factor of the size of the box than the ones we will compute. The exact computation needs the integral over a body, which we will meet in chapter 4, and gives the same result (CM (5.4.7), PDF p. 237, SADD §6.1, PDF p. 131). A computation with a box like ours is also done in EP §3.2.1 (pp. 105-106).

What do the two assumptions cost? Let us look at the first one with numbers. Let the steel bar of subsection 3.6.1 hang vertically, pulled at its lower end by a force of 10 kN, so that the stress in it is \(10\,000\ \text{N}/78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2 = 127{,}3\) MPa. Because of the bar's own weight the stress grows from the lower to the upper end, over 10 m, by \(\rho\,g\,L = 7800 \cdot 9{,}81 \cdot 10\ \text{Pa} = 0{,}765\) MPa. In the bar we imagine a box with the edge \(\Delta x = 1\) mm along the bar. From one of its faces to the opposite one the stress changes by \(7800 \cdot 9{,}81 \cdot 0{,}001\ \text{Pa} = 76{,}5\) Pa, which is \(6 \cdot 10^{-7}\) of the stress \(127{,}3\) MPa. This is the share of the work we leave out when we take the stress in the box as constant, and for a box half the size the share is half as large. The assumption is therefore good wherever the stress changes only by a small share over the length of the box, and such a box can always be chosen when the stress is a continuous function of position. It fails where the stress changes strongly over however short a distance, for example right at the sharp corner of a notch. The second assumption is of the same kind. It holds when the displacements are differentiable, because then the changes of displacement of opposite points differ almost exactly by the linear part, and the error is small compared with the edge of the box. It fails where the displacement jumps, for example across a crack.

First the two faces perpendicular to the \(x\) axis (figure 3.133).

  1. On the face with outward normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) take a small patch of area \(\Delta A\) around the point \(Q\). The force on it is \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\,\Delta A\) \(= (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}})\,\Delta A\) (equation (2.26)). On the opposite face, with outward normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), an equal patch around the point \(Q'\) lies straight across. By lemma 2.21 on the traction on the opposite side of a cut, the force on it is \(-\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\,\Delta A\). The two points differ only in the coordinate \(x\), by \(x_{\mathrm{Q}} - x_{\mathrm{Q}'} = \Delta x\).
  2. During the stage the two forces do the works \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\,\Delta A\cdot\Delta\vek u(Q)\) and \(-\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\,\Delta A\cdot\Delta\vek u(Q')\). By lemma 2.12 on the properties of the scalar product, items 2 and 3, their sum is
    \[\Delta A\,\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\cdot\big(\Delta\vek u(Q) - \Delta\vek u(Q')\big) .\]
    Only the difference of the changes of displacement of the two points counts. If both points moved equally, the work would be zero, because the two forces are opposite.
  3. In equation (3.64), written for \(Q\) and for \(Q'\), all terms are equal except the one with the coordinate \(x\). Hence \(\Delta u_{\mathrm{i}}(Q) - \Delta u_{\mathrm{i}}(Q') = \Delta H_{\mathrm{ix}}\,\Delta x\) for \(i = x, y, z\), or in short
    \[\Delta\vek u(Q) - \Delta\vek u(Q') = \Delta x\,(\Delta H_{\mathrm{xx}},\ \Delta H_{\mathrm{yx}},\ \Delta H_{\mathrm{zx}}) .\]
  4. We compute the scalar product by components (equation (2.6)). Each component of the force works on its own component of the difference. The component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\Delta A\) works on the difference along the \(x\) axis, \(\Delta x\,\Delta H_{\mathrm{xx}}\), by which the box gets longer during the stage. The component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\Delta A\) works on the difference along the \(y\) axis, \(\Delta x\,\Delta H_{\mathrm{yx}}\), by which the right face slides relative to the left one. The component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\Delta A\) works on the difference along the \(z\) axis, which the figure, drawn along this axis, does not show. The work of the pair of forces is
    \[\Delta A\,\Delta x\,\big(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\Delta H_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\Delta H_{\mathrm{yx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\Delta H_{\mathrm{zx}}\big) .\]
    It does not depend on where on the face the patch lies.
  5. We split the face into patches like the patch at \(Q\), each with its opposite patch, and add up the works of all pairs. The areas of the patches add up to the area of the face, \(\Delta y\,\Delta z\), which we multiply by the distance \(\Delta x\) between the two faces. Since \(\Delta y\,\Delta z\,\Delta x = \Delta V\), the work of the forces on the two faces perpendicular to the \(x\) axis is
    \[\Delta V\,\big(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\Delta H_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\Delta H_{\mathrm{yx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\Delta H_{\mathrm{zx}}\big) .\]
  6. We treat in the same way the faces perpendicular to the \(y\) axis, the top and the bottom one in figure 3.133, where \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}})\) and opposite points differ by \(\Delta y\) in the coordinate \(y\). The shear forces on them, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) to the right at the top and to the left at the bottom, are shown in figure 3.135 below. We treat the faces perpendicular to the \(z\) axis in the same way too. The work of the forces on all six faces is the sum of three such expressions:
    \[\begin{aligned} &\Delta V\,\big(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\Delta H_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\Delta H_{\mathrm{yx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\Delta H_{\mathrm{zx}} \\ &\qquad + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\Delta H_{\mathrm{xy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\Delta H_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\Delta H_{\mathrm{zy}} \\ &\qquad + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\Delta H_{\mathrm{xz}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}}\Delta H_{\mathrm{yz}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\Delta H_{\mathrm{zz}}\big) . \end{aligned}\]
  7. We write the normal terms with strains. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x\) (definition 1.121), \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{xx}} = \Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is the change of the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) during the stage: the lengthening of the box \(\Delta x\,\Delta H_{\mathrm{xx}}\) divided by its length \(\Delta x\). Likewise \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{yy}} = \Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{zz}} = \Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\).
  8. We group the shear terms in pairs with swapped indices. By theorem 2.41 on the symmetry of stress, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). By definition 1.121, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x)\), so \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{xy}} + \Delta H_{\mathrm{yx}} = 2\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The first term measures how far the top face slides relative to the bottom one, the second how far the right face slides relative to the left one. Together
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\Delta H_{\mathrm{yx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\Delta H_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,(\Delta H_{\mathrm{yx}} + \Delta H_{\mathrm{xy}}) = 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} .\]
    The same holds for the pairs with indices \(x\), \(z\) and \(y\), \(z\).
  9. The work of the forces on the faces of the box during the short stage is therefore
    \[\begin{aligned} &\Delta V\,\big(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} \\ &\qquad + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\big) = \Delta V \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} . \end{aligned} \tag{3.65}\]
    In the double sum the indices \(i\) and \(j\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), so the sum has nine terms. Each shear pair appears in it twice, for example as \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and as \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\), which are equal. Hence the factor two on the left.

Figure 3.134 builds the sum. In the grid the row belongs to the index \(i\) and the column to the index \(j\), and each cell is one term \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The three cells on the diagonal are the normal terms. The cells above the diagonal and below it are the shear terms, and the arrow joins the cells \(xy\) and \(yx\), which are equal: so every shear pair counts twice.

The work per unit volume during a short stage is therefore \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\)\(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). EP writes it the same way (p. 106). What has the computation shown?

First, a motion of the box as a whole does no work. In step 2 only the difference of the changes of displacement of opposite points counted, and the term \(\Delta u_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\) of equation (3.64) cancelled in step 3. The forces on opposite patches are opposite, and what one does in a common motion, the other takes away.

Second, a turn of the box does no work either. For a small turn about the \(z\) axis, \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{yx}} = -\Delta H_{\mathrm{xy}}\), which is the part of the gradient that describes the turn (definition 1.122). In step 8, however, \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{yx}}\) and \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{xy}}\) appear only in their sum, which is zero for a turn. Figure 3.135 shows why: the grey dashed square is the front face of the box in the \(xy\) plane before the stage, the orange quadrilateral the same face after it. In a counterclockwise turn (right) the right face moves up, the left one down, and the shear forces on them, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) up on the right and down on the left, do positive work. The top face, however, moves to the left, the bottom one to the right, and the shear forces on them, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) to the right at the top and to the left at the bottom, do negative work. The two works cancel exactly, because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\). The stresses therefore do work only through a change of strain, not through a motion or a turn.

Third, the factor two in the shear terms is not a convention but a consequence of the fact that in shear both pairs of faces work (figure 3.135, left). The right face moves up relative to the left one by \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\Delta x\), the top face to the right relative to the bottom one by \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\Delta y\), and each pair contributes its own work. In shear, where \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{xy}} = \Delta H_{\mathrm{yx}} = \Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), the two contributions are equal.

Let us test equation (3.65) on the bar of the previous subsection (figure 3.124). There only the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma\) is nonzero, so the work per unit volume during a short stage is \(\sigma\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), the stress times the change of strain. This is the same as the work of the force \(F = \sigma A\) over the motion of the end \(\Delta e = L\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), divided by the volume \(A L\).

During the whole loading the stresses change (figure 3.136), so we must add up the works of the short stages. We describe the loading with a parameter \(t\), for example time, running from \(t_0\) to \(t_1\). The strain and stress components at \(P\) are then functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(t)\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(t)\). We split the interval \([t_0, t_1]\) into short stages. During the stage from \(t_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) to \(t_{\mathrm{k}}\) the work per unit volume is, by equation (3.65), approximately

\[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(t_{\mathrm{k}-1})\,\big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(t_{\mathrm{k}}) - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(t_{\mathrm{k}-1})\big) .\]

By the mean value theorem 1.85 the change \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(t_{\mathrm{k}}) - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(t_{\mathrm{k}-1})\) equals \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}'(\xi_{\mathrm{ij},\mathrm{k}})\,(t_{\mathrm{k}} - t_{\mathrm{k}-1})\) for some number \(\xi_{\mathrm{ij},\mathrm{k}}\) between \(t_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) and \(t_{\mathrm{k}}\), which may be different for every component and every stage. The sum over the stages is therefore not exactly a Riemann sum of the function \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(t)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}'(t)\) (definition 3.47), which would take all parts of this function at the same point of the stage. It is close to one, though, and as the stages get shorter it approaches its integral. That it really does approach it would be shown with the uniform continuity of the stresses and of the derivatives of the strains as functions of the parameter (theorem 3.52), much as in the proof of theorem 3.53. We do not write this proof. EP writes the work per unit volume directly as an integral (EP (3.2.5), p. 103), while CM writes how fast this work grows, with the stress power (moč napetosti) (CM (5.4.11), PDF p. 238). We too define the work with an integral.

Definition 3.57 Work of the stresses per unit volume (delo napetosti na enoto prostornine)

Let \(P\) be a point of a body, and let the strain components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and the stress components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at \(P\) change during a loading with a parameter \(t\) from a closed interval \([t_0, t_1]\). Let the functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(t)\) be differentiable at every point of the interval \([t_0, t_1]\), at the endpoints with a one-sided derivative (definition 1.9), with derivatives continuous on \([t_0, t_1]\), and let the functions \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(t)\) be continuous on \([t_0, t_1]\). The work of the stresses per unit volume (delo napetosti na enoto prostornine) at \(P\) during this loading is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^{t_1} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(t)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t , \tag{3.66}\]
\[\int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^{t_1} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(t)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t , \tag{3.66}\]

where the indices \(i\) and \(j\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). If the loading consists of several successive stages, each with its own parameter, the work is the sum of the works of the stages.

Source: EP (3.2.4), (3.2.5) (p. 103) and (3.2.7) (p. 106), CM (5.4.11) (PDF p. 238), where the integrand \(\boldsymbol\sigma : \mathbf D\) is the stress power.

The integrand is a sum of nine terms, and each shear pair appears in it twice. Let us write it with the six different components. As in Voigt notation (definition 3.27), let \(\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\), \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) be the engineering shear strains. Then \(2\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}' = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}'\), and likewise for the other two pairs, so

\[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}' = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}' + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}' + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}' + \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}}' + \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}' + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}' . \tag{3.67}\]

The factor two has hidden itself in the engineering shear strain. This is why Voigt notation puts precisely the engineering shear strains into the column of strains: the integrand is the sum of the products of corresponding entries of the columns of definition 3.27

\[\{\sigma\} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}},\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}) , \qquad \{\varepsilon\} = (\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}},\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}},\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}},\ \gamma_{\mathrm{yz}},\ \gamma_{\mathrm{xz}},\ \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}) ,\]

which we write here in a row to save space. The entry of a column at place \(p\), where \(p\) is one of the numbers from \(1\) to \(6\), is written, as in the proof of lemma 3.31, \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\). Thus \(\{\varepsilon\}_1 = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\{\varepsilon\}_6 = \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\{\sigma\}_6 = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The braces keep us from confusing these with the principal stresses \(\sigma_1\), \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\). In this notation the integrand of equation (3.66) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{p}} \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}'\), where \(p\) runs from \(1\) to \(6\).

The simplest case is a uniaxial state, as in the bar, where only the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is nonzero. The strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) change too, in the steel bar both equal \(-\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), where \(\nu\) is Poisson's ratio (definition 3.8), but in the integrand (3.67) they are multiplied by the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\), so they add nothing to the work. We then take the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) itself as the parameter, running from \(0\) to the final value \(\varepsilon\). Its derivative with respect to the parameter is \(1\), so the work per unit volume is \(\int_0^{\varepsilon} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), the area under the curve of stress against strain (EP, p. 104), like the triangle in figure 3.126, left, except that there the axes carry the force and the elongation. In the steel bar \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), and the work is \(\int_0^{\varepsilon} E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12 E\,\varepsilon^2 = \tfrac12\,\sigma\,\varepsilon\), which is 41 356 J/m³ as before.

3.6.4 Ideal elastic material

We have defined the work per unit volume for every loading that ends at a given strain. Does it depend only on the final strain, or also on the path by which we got there? Above the yield stress the material did not give the work back (grey area), so the work depended on what had happened to the material, not only on the final strain. Let us show that it can depend on the path even for a material whose stresses are linear functions of the strains, as in equation (3.39).

Let only \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) change, while the other four strain components stay zero. Then by equation (3.67) only the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) do work. For a linear material they are

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = C_{11}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + C_{16}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = C_{61}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + C_{66}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} ,\]

where \(C_{11}\), \(C_{16}\), \(C_{61}\) and \(C_{66}\) are the entries of the material stiffness matrix in rows and columns \(1\) and \(6\) (definition 3.27). For steel \(C_{11} = \lambda + 2\mu = 263{,}8\) GPa, \(C_{66} = \mu = 75{,}38\) GPa and \(C_{16} = C_{61} = 0\), where \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) are the Lamé constants of steel (definition 3.18). Imagine a material that differs from steel only in that \(C_{16} = 10\) GPa, while \(C_{61}\) stays zero. In such a material the shear \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) causes a normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), but the stretch \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) causes no shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\).

Let us go from zero strain to the strain with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = a\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = b\), where \(a = b = 0{,}001\), along two paths (figure 3.138, left, with the directions of the axes \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) at the lower right). On the first path we first increase \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) from \(0\) to \(a\) at \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), to the point \(A\), then \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) from \(0\) to \(b\) at \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = a\). On the second path we first increase \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), to the point \(B\), then \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). On each leg of a path a single component changes, so we take it as the parameter \(t\), and its derivative with respect to the parameter is \(1\). We compute the integrals with the fundamental theorem of calculus and the function \(t^2/2\), whose derivative is \(t\). The constants \(C_{11}\) and \(C_{66}\) are rounded to four significant digits, so we round the works to four significant digits too. Each of these works is the area under the graph of the stress against the strain that changes on the leg. Figure 3.137 draws them: on the left \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) against \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) up to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = a\), on the right \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) against \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) up to \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = b\). The path in the plane of strains in figure 3.138 tells where we are, the areas in figure 3.137 tell how much work it costs.

  1. First path, first leg. The parameter is \(t = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) from \(0\) to \(a\), \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = C_{11}\,t\) and the work is \(\int_0^a C_{11}\,t\,\mathrm{d}t = \tfrac12 C_{11}\,a^2 = 131\,900\ \text{J/m}^3\). This is the area of the triangle under the line \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = C_{11}\,t\), which rises to \(C_{11}\,a = 263{,}8\) MPa.
  2. First path, second leg. The parameter is \(t = \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) from \(0\) to \(b\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = a\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = C_{61}\,a + C_{66}\,t\) and the work is \(\int_0^b (C_{61}\,a + C_{66}\,t)\,\mathrm{d}t = C_{61}\,a\,b + \tfrac12 C_{66}\,b^2 = 0 + 37\,690\ \text{J/m}^3\). This is the area of the triangle under the line \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = C_{66}\,t\), which rises to \(C_{66}\,b = 75{,}38\) MPa. Since \(C_{61} = 0\), the line starts at the origin.
  3. The work along the first path is the sum of the triangle and the triangle, \(131\,900 + 37\,690 = 169\,590\), rounded \(169\,600\ \text{J/m}^3\).
  4. Second path, first leg. The parameter is \(t = \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) from \(0\) to \(b\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = C_{66}\,t\) and the work is \(\tfrac12 C_{66}\,b^2 = 37\,690\ \text{J/m}^3\), the same triangle as in step 2.
  5. Second path, second leg. The parameter is \(t = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) from \(0\) to \(a\), \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = b\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = C_{11}\,t + C_{16}\,b\) and the work is \(\int_0^a (C_{11}\,t + C_{16}\,b)\,\mathrm{d}t = \tfrac12 C_{11}\,a^2 + C_{16}\,a\,b = 131\,900 + 10\,000 = 141\,900\ \text{J/m}^3\). The stress line is now lifted by \(C_{16}\,b = 10\) MPa above the line of step 1, and the work is the area of the triangle and of the strip above it together.
  6. The work along the second path is the sum of the triangle and the triangle with the band, \(37\,690 + 141\,900 = 179\,590\), rounded \(179\,600\ \text{J/m}^3\).

Both paths end at the same strain, but the second costs \(10\,000\) J/m³ more. The difference is \((C_{16} - C_{61})\,a\,b\), in figure 3.137 the grey strip: a parallelogram with the height \(C_{16}\,b = 10\) MPa and the width \(a = 0{,}001\), with the area \(10 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa} \cdot 0{,}001 = 10\,000\) J/m³. Where does it come from? On the second path \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) grows when the shear is already \(b\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) contains the part \(C_{16}\,b\), which acts over the whole way of length \(a\) and contributes \(C_{16}\,a\,b\). On the first path \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) grows when the stretch is already \(a\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) contains the part \(C_{61}\,a\), which would contribute \(C_{61}\,a\,b\), but is zero for our material.

Now we load the material along the first path and unload it along the second, from the end \(C\) back to the start \(O\) (figure 3.138, left). On the way back the stress at every strain has the same value as during loading along the same path, because it depends only on the strain, but the strain now changes in the opposite direction. Take the leg from \(C\) to \(B\) on which \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) returns from \(a\) to \(0\) at \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = b\). We describe it with a parameter \(t\) from \(0\) to \(a\) and with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = a - t\), whose derivative with respect to \(t\) is \(-1\). The function \(a\,t - t^2/2\) has the derivative \(a - t\), so the work is

\[\int_0^a \big(C_{11}\,(a - t) + C_{16}\,b\big)\cdot(-1)\,\mathrm{d}t = -\big(\tfrac12 C_{11}\,a^2 + C_{16}\,a\,b\big) ,\]

the opposite of the work on the same leg during loading. The same holds on the other leg. Unloading along the second path, the material therefore gives back about \(179\,600\) J/m³, while loading along the first path it received only about \(169\,600\) J/m³. After the round trip the material is in the same state as at the start, but it has given its surroundings \(10\,000\) J/m³ more than it received. A piece with a volume of one cubic decimetre, \(10^{-3}\) m³, would deliver 10 J of work in every round trip without anything being used up anywhere.

No such material exists. The second law of thermodynamics requires that in every cycle of deformation that ends at the same strain and the same internal energy as it started, the total work done on the material is positive or zero, when the cycle takes place at constant temperature or without heat exchange with the surroundings (BOWER §3.1.1, PDF p. 93). The internal energy (notranja energija) is the energy that a substance keeps within itself, in the small motions of its molecules and in its deformation (CM §5.4.2, PDF p. 236). The round trip in the opposite direction, loading along the second path and unloading along the first, gives the work \(+10\,000\) J/m³ and does not contradict this law, but the round trip in our direction does. For a material whose stress depends only on the current strain, the round trip in the opposite direction has the opposite work: on every leg the stress at every strain is the same, but the changes of strain have the opposite sign, as we computed on the leg above. The second law requires the work of both round trips to be positive or zero, so the work of both is zero. Any two paths from zero strain to the same strain, the first out and the second back, form such a round trip, so the work along both paths is the same. The general proof needs entropy (entropija), a thermodynamic quantity that we will not use in this book, so we do not develop it (CM §6.1.4, PDF pp. 253-254).

Let us say the same property once more in the words of that proof, because this is how the lectures say it. The second law says that entropy can be produced in a substance but cannot vanish: the quantity that CM calls the entropy production (nastajanje entropije) is never negative (CM (5.4.23) and (5.4.24), PDF p. 240). It is produced whenever work turns irreversibly into heat, as when we rub our palms together. A process in which this internal dissipation (notranja izguba) is zero is reversible (povraten), otherwise it is irreversible (CM, PDF pp. 239 and 240). A reversible process can be run backwards through the same states, so that in the end both the material and its surroundings are as they were at the start. Loading and unloading an ideal elastic material is such a process: along the same path out and back the material returns all the work it received, no work turns into heat and no entropy is produced. When the material exchanges no heat with its surroundings meanwhile, its entropy does not change at all (CM, PDF p. 239). This is the meaning of the statement that in an ideal elastic material the entropy does not grow during deformation. Steel above the yield stress is the opposite case. The grey area in figure 3.126, right, is work that has turned into heat. The entropy has grown, and this process cannot be run backwards.

We take the property we found with the cycle as a definition.

For the definition we still need an agreement on which strains are small. In what follows, a small strain is a strain for which each of the six components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}}\), \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is smaller in absolute value than a chosen bound, for example \(0{,}0011\), which on the strain axis means a band around zero. With this bound a tension test of steel stays below the strain at the yield stress, \(220\ \text{MPa}/196\ \text{GPa} = 0{,}00112\), and the strains of size \(0{,}001\) that we compute with in this section are small. A function of the six strain components is continuous if it satisfies definition 1.68, except that the distance is measured between two columns of six numbers instead of between two points with three coordinates. The distance between two columns is the square root of the sum of the squares of the differences of corresponding entries (LEBL1 Example 7.1.5, PDF p. 258, and Def. 7.5.1, PDF p. 288).

Definition 3.58 Ideal elastic material (idealno elastičen material)

A material is ideal elastic (idealno elastičen) at a point \(P\) if two things hold.

  1. Each stress component at \(P\) is a function of the six strain components at \(P\), continuous at all small strains, that is, strains whose components are all smaller in absolute value than a chosen bound. At zero strain all stress components are zero.
  2. The work of the stresses per unit volume (definition 3.57) in every loading that meets the conditions of that definition, starts at zero strain and runs through small strains depends only on the strain at which the loading ends, not on the path along which the strain changed.

Source: BOWER §3.2.7 (PDF p. 102), where the work done to deform the material depends only on the final strain, and §3.1.1 (PDF p. 93), SADD §6.1 (PDF pp. 128 and 130-131). CM calls the first item Cauchy elasticity (CM §6.2.1, PDF p. 255).

Figure 3.140, left, is the graph of stress against strain of an ideal elastic material: the curve passes through zero strain, around it is the band of small strains, and at the strain \(\varepsilon_1\) the point on the curve has a single stress \(\sigma_1\). On the right is a loop, where the same strain has two stresses that depend on the path, which the first item forbids.

The first item says that the material has no memory: the stress at a given strain is always the same, no matter how the material got there. The second item is the requirement we found with the cycle. A material that does not satisfy it, like our imagined material with \(C_{16} \ne C_{61}\), could deliver work from nothing in a cycle, \(10\,000\) J/m³ per round trip. In the lectures the material is called gradivo, so an ideal elastic material is idealno elastično gradivo.

The first item says one more thing: the material does not lag. There is no time in the law, so the stress at some instant belongs to the strain at the same instant, whatever happened before and however fast anything changes. Figure 3.141, left, shows this on a test in which we raise the stress, hold it for a while and remove it again. The upper graph is the stress against time \(t\), the lower one the strain against time. In an ideal elastic material the strain has at every instant the value that belongs to the current stress. At the instant \(t_0\), when the stress reaches its full value, so does the strain. From the instant \(t_1\) on it falls with the stress, and when the stress is zero, the strain is zero too. The lectures say this with the word hipoma (instantly): the body deforms under the load without delay and returns to its original state without delay after unloading.

The near miss is a material that lags (the grey dashed curve). When the stress is already full, the strain still falls short. While the stress is held it creeps slowly towards the final value, and after unloading it returns only slowly. Crosslinked polymers behave like this: BOWER states that after the load is removed they eventually return to their original shape, but this can take a very long time (BOWER §3.6.1, PDF p. 133). Such a material does return in the end, and yet it is not ideal elastic. While the stress is held it is the same all the time, but the strain is one value at the instant \(t_0\) and another a little later. So the stress is not a function of the strain alone, and item 1 fails. These are the viscoelastic materials of section 3.1.9.

In this book we loaded the bar slowly, while the lectures assume that loading and unloading happen instantly. The two demands do not oppose each other, because they speak of two things. The word instantly speaks of the material at a point: the strain follows the stress without delay. The word slowly speaks of the body as a whole: the load must change more slowly than the waves settle through the body, so that the body is in equilibrium at every instant. Why this is right and what it costs we computed in subsection 3.6.1: in our bar the stresses settle in \(0{,}032\) s, and if we stretch it in one second, only a millionth of the work goes into motion. It fails in an impact, when the load changes faster than in these hundredths of a second. Then a part of the work stays in the motion, and the mass enters the equations too. The two demands together say the same thing: time does not appear in the law. This is why the parameter \(t\) in definition 3.57 can be anything that numbers the states of the loading, and in the computation along the two paths we took the strain itself for it.

To these two demands, response without delay and independence of the path, the lectures add a third assumption: the body does not lose stability during loading, that is, it does not snap into another shape. What this means is shown by a slender straight bar between two pins, which we compress along its axis with the force \(P\) (figure 3.141, right). Let us try it with a ruler between our palms. For a while it resists and stays straight, then it bulges sideways. This is the buckling of section 3.3.3. Our steel bar, 10 m long and 10 mm thick, buckles between pins already at a compressive force of about \(9{,}5\) N, as we stated there, while in tension it carries 10 kN, more than a thousand times as much.

Why do we need this assumption if the material at every point is still ideal elastic? Because it speaks of the body, not of the material. Below the critical force the bar has at every force a single equilibrium shape, the straight one, and this shape changes continuously with the force. Above the critical force the straight shape is no longer stable. The bar bends, to the left or to the right, and a small chance disturbance decides which. The load then no longer determines the deformation. Some bodies even jump when they lose stability. The metal lid of a jar, pressed in the middle, clicks into a dented shape at a certain force: there is no equilibrium shape nearby any more, so it moves far and fast, although we press slowly. During such a snap-through (preskok) the body is not in equilibrium (COOK §18.1, PDF p. 656, and §17.2, PDF p. 613). A part of the work goes into motion, which we hear as the click and which dies out through vibration into heat. This part does not come back, although the material is ideal elastic. When does the assumption hold? In tension below the yield stress always, in compression as long as the force is below the critical one. For stocky bodies it therefore almost never decides, for slender bars, thin plates and shells in compression it must be checked. What does it give? With it a single deformation belongs to every load, the body passes through equilibrium states only, and all the work of the external forces is stored in the material. Without it, the computation with the straight shape would predict for our bar at 10 kN of compression a shortening of \(6{,}496\) mm, while in truth the bar buckles already at a thousandth of this force. We treat the stability of equilibrium, buckling and snap-through in chapter 8 (section 8.14 and figure 8.77).

Since for an ideal elastic material the work depends only on the final strain, it is a function of this strain.

Definition 3.59 Strain energy density (gostota deformacijske energije)

Let the material at the point \(P\) be ideal elastic. The strain energy density (gostota deformacijske energije) \(w\) at \(P\) at a small strain \(\{\varepsilon\}\) is the work of the stresses per unit volume in any loading that meets the conditions of definition 3.57, starts at zero strain, runs through small strains and ends at the strain \(\{\varepsilon\}\):

\[w(\{\varepsilon\}) = \int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^{t_1} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(t)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t . \tag{3.68}\]
\[w(\{\varepsilon\}) = \int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^{t_1} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(t)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t . \tag{3.68}\]

Source: EP (3.2.7) (p. 106), SADD (6.1.3), (6.1.7) (PDF pp. 129 and 131), BOWER §3.2.7 (PDF p. 102).

Figure 3.142, left, is the graph of stress against strain: the straight line leaves zero strain, the triangle under it is \(w\), and on unloading it returns along the same line. On the right is the column of internal energy, divided into the free part and the part tied to entropy.

The strain energy density is a number that depends on the six strain components, so a function of six variables, and its unit is J/m³, which is the same as Pa. At zero strain \(w = 0\), because a loading that does not leave zero strain does no work: the derivatives of the strains are zero, and so is the integral. The name says what the number means: the material received it as work during loading and keeps it (area of the triangle) until it gives it back on unloading. Thermodynamics also tells which energy this is. In loading without heat exchange \(w\) is the increase of the internal energy per unit volume, in loading at constant temperature the increase of the Helmholtz free energy (Helmholtzova prosta energija), which is the internal energy reduced by a part tied to entropy (CM (5.4.11), PDF p. 238, CM (5.4.26), PDF p. 240, CM §6.2.2, PDF pp. 255-256). CM denotes it by \(\Psi\) and writes \(\Psi = e - \theta\,\eta\), where \(e\) is the internal energy and \(\eta\) the entropy, both per unit mass, and \(\theta\) the temperature. Why free? In a reversible process at constant temperature the increase of \(\Psi\), multiplied by the density, equals the work of the stresses per unit volume (CM (5.4.27), PDF p. 240). So this is the part of the energy that we can get back as work. For small strains the Helmholtz free energy is the same as the strain energy density (CM §6.2.3, PDF p. 256). In the lectures the Helmholtz free energy per unit volume is written \(\Psi\) and also \(W\), which is our \(w\). We keep the lower-case letter, because \(W\) is a weight in this book (equation (2.1)), and the letter \(\Psi\) will be needed for a map. For small strains EP assumes constant temperature and calls \(w\) simply the stored elastic energy per unit volume (EP §3.2.1, p. 102). For the computations in this book we do not need this distinction, because we always compute \(w\) from the stresses and strains.

The bar of subsection 3.6.1 is made of steel, which is ideal elastic below the yield stress, and for it \(w = \tfrac12 E\,\varepsilon^2 = \tfrac12\,\sigma\,\varepsilon\), the area of the triangle under the stress line, like the triangle in figure 3.137, only with \(E\) in place of \(C_{11}\). How much energy is that? Take steel at a strain of \(\varepsilon = 0{,}001\) in a tension test. The stress is then \(\sigma = E\,\varepsilon = 196\) MPa, still below the yield stress, and

\[w = \tfrac12 E\,\varepsilon^2 = \tfrac12 \cdot 196 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa} \cdot (0{,}001)^2 = 98\,000\ \text{J/m}^3 .\]

One cubic decimetre of such steel, \(10^{-3}\) m³, stores 98 J. That is the work it takes to lift a kilogram by about 10 m, since \(1\ \text{kg} \cdot 9{,}81\ \text{m/s}^2 \cdot 10\ \text{m} = 98{,}1\) J. Per unit mass, as CM measures energy, this is \(98\,000\ \text{J/m}^3 / 7800\ \text{kg/m}^3 = 12{,}6\) J/kg. The density grows with the square of the strain, because the stress and the strain grow together and \(w\) is half their product. For a material that stayed linear, twice the strain would therefore give four times the density. Steel at a strain of \(0{,}002\), however, would already be above the yield stress, where the formula \(\tfrac12 E\,\varepsilon^2\) no longer holds.

3.6.5 Stresses from the energy

In the bar of section 3.5 the force told how fast the work grows with the elongation: the work up to the elongation \(e\) is \(\tfrac12 k\,e^2\), the area of the triangle under the line of the force in figure 3.126, and its derivative with respect to \(e\) is the force \(k\,e\). For an ideal elastic material it is the same, except that there are six variables. A material whose stresses are in this way derivatives of some function of the strain has a special name.

From history

In 1837 Green wrote a paper on the reflection and refraction of light at the surface between two media (LOVE, PDF p. 28). For the calculation he had to know how a vibration travels through the ether, the substance then believed to carry light (TIMO, PDF p. 190). He did not know how the particles of the ether act on each other, and he did not want to adopt molecular assumptions, because nature may behave quite differently (TIMO, PDF p. 191). He took a general principle instead: however the parts of a system act on each other, the sum of all internal forces multiplied by the small displacements is, for any part of the mass, the change of a single function (TIMO, PDF p. 191). This is the requirement that energy is conserved, since otherwise the work of the internal forces would depend on the path and a material, returned to the same state, could give out work. He expanded the function in the strain components. The term of first degree drops out, because an undeformed body must have the smallest energy, and the terms of third and higher degree are negligible for small strains (LOVE, PDF p. 28-29). What remains is a sum of terms, each of which is a product of two strain components and a number (TIMO, PDF p. 191). In general there are 21 such terms, six squares and 15 products of two different components, and for a body that is the same in all directions only two numbers remain (TIMO, PDF p. 191). William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, justified the existence of such a function in 1855 by the first and second laws of thermodynamics: when a solid is deformed without a change of temperature, the stress components are derivatives of a function of the strain components (LOVE, PDF p. 29).

Let us return to a material whose stresses are derivatives of one function of the strain components, as for a bar the force is the derivative of work with respect to the elongation. The following definition describes it exactly.

Definition 3.60 Green-elastic material (Green-elastičen material)

A material is Green-elastic (Green-elastičen) or hyperelastic (hiperelastičen) at a point \(P\) if there is a function \(w\) of the six strain components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}}\), \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), defined at all small strains, with the value zero at zero strain, whose partial derivatives are the stress components at \(P\):

\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{\partial w}{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}} , & \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} &= \frac{\partial w}{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}} , & \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} &= \frac{\partial w}{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}} , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} &= \frac{\partial w}{\partial\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}}} , & \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} &= \frac{\partial w}{\partial\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}} , & \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \frac{\partial w}{\partial\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}} . \end{aligned} \tag{3.69}\]
\[\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \frac{\partial w}{\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}} , \qquad i, j = x, y, z . \tag{3.69}\]

Source: CM §6.2.2, (6.2.15) (PDF pp. 255 and 257), SADD (6.1.12) (PDF p. 132), EP (3.2.6) (p. 103), BOWER (PDF p. 104).

The partial derivative of a function of six variables is defined in the same way as for three variables (definition 1.26): we change one variable, hold the other five fixed, and take the limit of the difference quotient (LEBL2 Def. 8.3.8, PDF p. 39, for functions of \(n\) variables). Why do we differentiate with respect to \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and not \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\)?
