When the shear strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) grows by \(\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\) grows by the same amount, because it is the same number, and on the square of figure 3.135, left, both pairs of shear forces do work. By equation (3.65) the work per unit volume grows by \(2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\Delta\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The energy density therefore grows at the rate \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) per unit change of \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), or at the rate \(2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) per unit change of \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The sources write \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \partial w/\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) for all nine components (CM (6.2.15), PDF p. 257, SADD (6.1.12), PDF p. 132). The index form of equation (3.69) is written this way too. They treat \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\) as two variables and write \(w\) as a sum over all nine components, symmetric in \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\) (CM (6.3.1), PDF p. 258, SADD (6.1.9), PDF p. 131). If we change only \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and hold \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\) fixed, such a sum changes by half the work \(2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), and the derivative is again \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). Both ways give the same stresses. We use six variables with engineering shear strains to stay clear of this trap.

Let us also see what the definition rejects. The imagined material from section 3.6.4, which differs from steel only by \(C_{16} = 10\) GPa at \(C_{61} = 0\), is not Green-elastic if no function \(w\) satisfies the equations (3.69). Let us show that this is so, for deformations in which only \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are different from zero, that is, in the plane of figure 3.138, left.

  1. Suppose \(w\) exists. Let \(f(x, y)\) be the value of \(w\) at the deformation with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = x\), \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = y\) and the other four components zero. By the definition, \(\partial f/\partial x = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = C_{11}\,x + C_{16}\,y\) and \(\partial f/\partial y = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = C_{61}\,x + C_{66}\,y\).
  2. The mixed derivatives are \(\partial^2 f/\partial y\,\partial x = C_{16} = 10\) GPa and \(\partial^2 f/\partial x\,\partial y = C_{61} = 0\). The first tells how much normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) a unit of shear adds, the second how much shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) a unit of stretch adds. They exist everywhere and are constant, so they are continuous.
  3. By theorem 1.131 on the interchange of mixed derivatives (with a third variable on which \(f\) does not depend) they would be equal. They differ by \(10\) GPa, so the function \(w\) does not exist and the material is not Green-elastic. This is the same difference \((C_{16} - C_{61})\,a\,b\) by which, in figure 3.138, the works along the first and the second path to the same strain \(C\) differ, and that in section 3.6.4 gave \(10\,000\) J/m³ of work from nothing.

If we also set \(C_{61} = 10\) GPa, the derivatives are equal, \(10\) GPa, and the function \(w = \tfrac12 C_{11}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + C_{16}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} + \tfrac12 C_{66}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2\) is suitable: \(\partial w/\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = C_{11}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + C_{16}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\partial w/\partial\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = C_{16}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + C_{66}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). Each stress separately is the derivative of some function already at \(C_{61} = 0\). The definition rejects the requirement that a single function \(w\) be the source of both stresses at once.

Now let us show that every ideal elastic material is Green-elastic, and that the function \(w\) is precisely the strain energy density. The idea is the same as for the bar. Let us draw it (figure 3.143, left). The horizontal axis carries the component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), the vertical one the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), and the other strain components are held fixed. The curve \(f\) shows how the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) changes as we increase \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) alone. We start at a value smaller by \(r_0\) than the value at the strain \(\{\varepsilon\}\), where the stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The work per unit volume on this piece of the path is the grey area under the curve, as for the bar the work was the area under the line of the force. When we go on by \(r\), to the new value, the area grows by the blue strip. The strip is almost the rectangle with sides \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(r\). It differs from it only by the orange sliver at the top, which for a small \(r\) is much smaller than the rectangle. The added work is therefore about \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,r\).

The middle part of figure 3.143 shows the same, with the energy density \(w\) on the vertical axis. The curve \(w\) rises with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). From the value at the strain \(\{\varepsilon\}\) to the value at the component larger by \(r\) it rises by \(\Delta w\), the area of the blue strip. As \(r\) gets smaller, the quotient \(\Delta w/r\) approaches the slope of the tangent, the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The stress is the slope of the energy. This is exactly what item 2 of the fundamental theorem of calculus says: the derivative of an integral with respect to its upper limit is the integrand. We will use the right part of the figure at theorem 3.62.

Lemma 3.61 Stress as the derivative of the energy density (napetost kot odvod gostote energije)

Let the material at the point \(P\) be ideal elastic, and let \(w\) be its strain energy density. Then at every small strain \(w\) has partial derivatives with respect to all six strain components and satisfies equations (3.69), where the left sides are the stress components at this strain. The material is therefore Green-elastic.

Proof

We must show that the derivative of \(w\) with respect to each strain component is the corresponding stress component. We write the proof for the component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), for the others it is the same.

  1. Let \(\{\varepsilon\}\) be a small strain. All its components are smaller in absolute value than the chosen bound, so there is a number \(r_0 > 0\) such that \(|\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}| + r_0\) is also smaller than the bound. For a number \(s\) with \(-r_0 \le s \le r_0\) let \(\{\varepsilon\}(s)\) be the strain that has the component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + s\) and the other components equal to those of \(\{\varepsilon\}\). All these strains are small, and \(\{\varepsilon\}(0) = \{\varepsilon\}\).
  2. Let \(-r_0 < r < r_0\). We reach the strain \(\{\varepsilon\}(r)\) with a loading in two stages (figure 3.138, right). In the first stage we go from zero strain to \(\{\varepsilon\}(-r_0)\) along any path through small strains, for example straight, \(t\,\{\varepsilon\}(-r_0)\) for \(t\) from \(0\) to \(1\). In the second stage we go through the strains \(\{\varepsilon\}(s)\) in the direction of the component \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\), here \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), as \(s\) runs from \(-r_0\) to \(r\): the stretch of length \(r_0\) up to the strain \(\{\varepsilon\}\) and then the stretch of length \(r\), together on the straight part of the path. The path must meet the conditions of the definition of the work of the stresses 3.57.
  3. In this step and the next two we show that the straight first stage and the second stage meet these conditions. On both, the strain at the parameter \(t\) is \(\{\alpha\} + t\,\{\beta\}\), where \(\{\alpha\}\) and \(\{\beta\}\) are fixed columns of six numbers. In the first stage \(\{\alpha\}\) has all components zero and \(\{\beta\}\) is \(\{\varepsilon\}(-r_0)\). In the second stage, where we call the parameter \(s\), \(\{\alpha\} = \{\varepsilon\}\), and the column \(\{\beta\}\) has the component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) equal to \(1\) and the others zero. Each strain component is therefore a fixed number plus a fixed number times the parameter, and it is differentiable with a constant, hence continuous, derivative. All these strains are small. In the first stage no component is larger in absolute value than the corresponding component of the small strain \(\{\varepsilon\}(-r_0)\), and in the second stage all the strains \(\{\varepsilon\}(s)\) with \(-r_0 \le s \le r_0\) are small by step 1.
  4. The distance between the strains at the parameters \(t\) and \(t'\) of the same stage is \(|t - t'|\,d\), where \(d\) is the distance of the column \(\{\beta\}\) from zero strain. Indeed, corresponding components differ by \(t - t'\) times the corresponding component of \(\{\beta\}\). The sum of the squares of the differences is therefore \((t - t')^2\) times the sum of the squares of the components of \(\{\beta\}\), which is \(d^2\), and its square root is \(|t - t'|\,d\).
  5. Each stress component is a continuous function of the parameter in both stages. Choose \(t\) and \(\eta > 0\). By item 1 of the definition of an ideal elastic material 3.58 the stress component is continuous at the small strain \(\{\alpha\} + t\,\{\beta\}\), so there is \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that its value at every small strain whose distance from \(\{\alpha\} + t\,\{\beta\}\) is less than \(\delta_1\) differs from its value at \(\{\alpha\} + t\,\{\beta\}\) by less than \(\eta\). We take \(\delta = \delta_1/(d + 1)\). For a parameter \(t'\) of the same stage with \(|t' - t| < \delta\) the distance is, by step 4, \(|t' - t|\,d \le \delta\,d < \delta_1\), so the values of the stress at \(t'\) and at \(t\) differ by less than \(\eta\). In the second stage this holds for all \(s\) with \(-r_0 \le s \le r_0\).
  6. The previous three steps show that the path meets these conditions. By item 2 of the definition of an ideal elastic material 3.58 and by the definition of the strain energy density 3.59, the work along this path therefore equals \(w(\{\varepsilon\}(r))\), and the work of the first stage equals \(w(\{\varepsilon\}(-r_0))\). By the definition of the work of the stresses 3.57, the work along the whole path is the sum of the works of the two stages.
  7. In the second stage the parameter is \(s\). The component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + s\) and has the derivative \(1\), the other components are constant and have the derivative \(0\). By equation (3.67) only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is left of the integrand, the stress at the strain \(\{\varepsilon\}(s)\), which we call \(f(s)\). The work of the second stage is therefore \(\int_{-\mathrm{r}_0}^{r} f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\), the area under the curve \(f\) in figure 3.143, left, and by step 6
    \[w(\{\varepsilon\}(r)) = w(\{\varepsilon\}(-r_0)) + \int_{-\mathrm{r}_0}^{r} f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s .\]
  8. By step 5 the function \(f\) is continuous on \([-r_0, r_0]\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.55, item 2, on the interval \([-r_0, r_0]\), the function \(r \mapsto \int_{-\mathrm{r}_0}^{r} f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\) is therefore differentiable at the interior point \(r = 0\) with the derivative \(f(0)\), the height of the curve at the strain \(\{\varepsilon\}\). The first term on the right in step 7 does not depend on \(r\) and has the derivative zero (lemma 1.82). The function \(r \mapsto w(\{\varepsilon\}(r))\) therefore has the derivative \(f(0)\) at \(r = 0\), the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) at the strain \(\{\varepsilon\}\).
  9. The function \(r \mapsto w(\{\varepsilon\}(r))\) is \(w\) in which only the component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) changes while the others are held fixed. Its derivative at \(r = 0\), the slope of the tangent to the curve \(w\), is therefore the partial derivative \(\partial w/\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) at the strain \(\{\varepsilon\}\). Hence \(\partial w/\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\).
  10. For another component we repeat steps 1 to 9 with that component instead of \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). For a shear component, for example \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), what is left of the integrand (3.67) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}'\) with the derivative \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}' = 1\), so we get \(\partial w/\partial\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\).

Source: SADD (6.1.12) (PDF p. 132) states the claim and leaves the proof to an exercise, CM §6.2.2 (PDF pp. 255-256) derives it from thermodynamics. The proof with a path in two stages is not from the sources.

The proof has shown why the stress is the derivative of the energy. When we increase the component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) by a small \(r\), the material receives additional work of about \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,r\) per unit volume, the blue strip in figure 3.143. In the bar this meant that the force tells how much work the next tenth of a millimetre of elongation adds: at the force \(F_1 = 10\) kN about \(10\,000\ \text{N} \cdot 0.0001\ \text{m} = 1\) J.

Let us test it on the steel of section 3.6.4, with \(C_{11} = 263.8\) GPa, when only the component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is different from zero. Then \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = C_{11}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(w = \tfrac12 C_{11}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\). At \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0.001\) the stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 263.8\) MPa and the energy density is \(w = 131\,900\ \text{J/m}^3\). We increase the component by \(r\) and compute the increase \(\Delta w\), the difference of the values of \(w\) at \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + r\) and at \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\):

\[\begin{aligned} r &= 0.0001: & \Delta w &= 27\,699\ \text{J/m}^3 , & \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,r &= 26\,380\ \text{J/m}^3 , & \Delta w/r &= 277.0\ \text{MPa} , \\ r &= 0.00001: & \Delta w &= 2651.19\ \text{J/m}^3 , & \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,r &= 2638\ \text{J/m}^3 , & \Delta w/r &= 265.1\ \text{MPa} . \end{aligned}\]

The rectangle \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,r\) misses the increase by the sliver \(\tfrac12 C_{11}\,r^2\), the first time by \(1319\ \text{J/m}^3\), the second time by \(13.19\ \text{J/m}^3\). With \(r\) ten times smaller the sliver is a hundred times smaller and the rectangle only ten times, so the quotient \(\Delta w/r\) approaches the stress \(263.8\) MPa.

Where did the two requirements of ideal elasticity enter the proof? The independence of the work from the path (item 2 of definition 3.58) entered in step 6. Without it the work up to the strain \(\{\varepsilon\}(r)\) would not be a single number \(w\), and there would be nothing to differentiate. In the imagined material with \(C_{16} = 10\) GPa and \(C_{61} = 0\) the works along the two paths to the same strain differ by \(10\,000\ \text{J/m}^3\), about \(6\,\%\) of the work \(169\,600\ \text{J/m}^3\) along the first path. The continuity of the stresses (item 1) entered in step 8. If the stress jumped at the strain \(\{\varepsilon\}\), the curve \(w\) would have a kink there, with one slope on the left and another on the right, and there would be no derivative.

The converse holds too, provided the stresses, that is, the partial derivatives of \(w\), are continuous functions of the strain and zero at zero strain: such a Green-elastic material is ideal elastic, since the work along any path is the difference of the values of \(w\) at its ends. Item 1 of the definition of an ideal elastic material 3.58 asks for both conditions, while the definition of a Green-elastic material 3.60 does not contain them. EP calls such stresses conservative (EP §3.2.1, p. 103). The proof would need a rule for the derivative of a function of several variables along a path, which the book does not have yet, so we do not write it.

Now we can keep the promise of section 3.4. Let the material be linear elastic, with stresses that are linear functions of the strains, \(\{\sigma\} = \mat C\,\{\varepsilon\}\), where \(\mat C\) is the material stiffness matrix with entries \(C_{\mathrm{pq}}\), or entry by entry

\[\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}} = \sum_{\mathrm{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}} , \qquad p = 1, \dots, 6 ,\]

where \(q\) runs from \(1\) to \(6\). If such a material is ideal elastic, then by lemma 3.61 on the stress as the derivative of the energy density \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}} = \partial w/\partial\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\). The derivative of this stress with respect to the component \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}\) is \(C_{\mathrm{pq}}\). The derivative of the stress \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{q}}\) with respect to the component \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\) is \(C_{\mathrm{qp}}\). Both are mixed derivatives of the same function \(w\), once first with respect to \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\) and then \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}\), once in the opposite order, and by theorem 1.131 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives they are equal.

Theorem 3.62 Symmetry of the elastic constants (simetrija elastičnih konstant)

Let the material at the point \(P\) be ideal elastic and linear elastic, so that at every small strain \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}} = \sum_{\mathrm{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}\) for \(p = 1, \dots, 6\), with the entries \(C_{\mathrm{pq}}\) of the material stiffness matrix \(\mat C\). Then:

  1. the matrix \(\mat C\) is symmetric, \(C_{\mathrm{pq}} = C_{\mathrm{qp}}\) for all \(p\) and \(q\) from \(1\) to \(6\), so the elastic constants satisfy \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{klij}}\) for all indices \(i\), \(j\), \(k\) and \(l\) running over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\),
  2. the strain energy density at the strain \(\{\varepsilon\}\) is
\[w = \frac12 \sum_{\mathrm{p}} \sum_{\mathrm{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}} = \frac12 \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} . \tag{3.70}\]
\[w = \frac12\,C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}} = \frac12\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} . \tag{3.70}\]
Proof

We must show the symmetry of the matrix and the formula for \(w\). The first follows from the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives, the second from the work along a straight path.

1. Symmetry.

  1. By lemma 3.61 on the stress as the derivative of the energy density, at every small strain \(\partial w/\partial\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}} = \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} C_{\mathrm{pr}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{r}}\), where \(r\) runs from \(1\) to \(6\).
  2. Let \(p \ne q\). If we increase the component \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}\) by \(h\) and hold the others fixed, \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\) increases by exactly \(C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,h\). The difference quotient is therefore \(C_{\mathrm{pq}}\) for every \(h \ne 0\), and its limit is \(C_{\mathrm{pq}}\). The mixed derivative of \(w\), first with respect to \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\) and then \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}\), therefore exists at every small strain and equals the constant \(C_{\mathrm{pq}}\). Likewise the mixed derivative in the opposite order equals \(C_{\mathrm{qp}}\).
  3. Choose a small strain and hold the four components other than \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}\) at its values. Let \(f(x, y, z)\) be the value of \(w\) at the strain with \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}} = x\) and \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}} = y\). This is a function of three variables that does not depend on \(z\). It is defined around the point \((\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}, \{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}, 0)\), its partial derivatives with respect to \(x\) and \(y\) are the stresses \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{q}}\), and its mixed derivatives are the constants \(C_{\mathrm{pq}}\) and \(C_{\mathrm{qp}}\), hence continuous.
  4. By theorem 1.131 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives, the two mixed derivatives of \(f\) are equal, so \(C_{\mathrm{pq}} = C_{\mathrm{qp}}\). For \(p = q\) the equality only says that a number equals itself.
  5. The pairs \(ij\) and \(kl\) are the places \(p\) and \(q\) (definition 3.27). Swapping indices within a pair does not change the constant (lemma 3.26), so step 4 gives, for all orders,
    \[C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{pq}} = C_{\mathrm{qp}} = C_{\mathrm{klij}} .\]

2. Energy density.

  1. By definition 3.59 we may compute \(w\) along any path from zero strain to \(\{\varepsilon\}\). Take the straight path \(t\,\{\varepsilon\}\) as \(t\) runs from \(0\) to \(1\) (figure 3.143, right). All its strains are small, because \(|t\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}| \le |\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}|\).
  2. On this path the strain component \(p\) is \(t\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\), with the derivative \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\) with respect to \(t\), and the stress is \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,t\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}\), a straight line from zero to the final value \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\). Both are a fixed number times \(t\), so the path meets the conditions of the definition of the work of the stresses 3.57: the strain components have constant derivatives, and the stresses are continuous.
  3. By equation (3.67) the integrand equals \(\sum_{\mathrm{p}} \sum_{\mathrm{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,t\), a constant number times \(t\). The integral \(\int_0^1 t\,\mathrm{d}t = \tfrac12\) is the area of the triangle under the line with the final value \(1\). By the linearity of the integral (lemma 3.54, item 1) and the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.55 with the function \(t^2/2\),
    \[w = \sum_{\mathrm{p}} \sum_{\mathrm{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}} \int_0^1 t\,\mathrm{d}t = \frac12 \sum_{\mathrm{p}} \sum_{\mathrm{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}} .\]
  4. The inner sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}\) is \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\), so \(w = \tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{p}} \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\). By equation (3.67), applied to products instead of derivatives, this is \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\).

Source: CM (6.3.1)-(6.3.3), (6.3.5) (PDF p. 258), SADD (6.1.13), (6.1.14) (PDF p. 132) and (6.1.7) (PDF p. 131), BOWER (PDF p. 104), EP (3.2.11) (p. 107). Replacing the function of six variables by a function of three variables in step 3 is not from the sources. LEBL2 Prop. 8.6.2 (PDF p. 60) swaps mixed derivatives for functions of any number of variables.

The stiffness matrix of an ideal elastic material is therefore symmetric, and only the entries on and above the diagonal are different, \(6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 21\). A material whose inner structure has no symmetry at all needs all 21 constants, as we announced in section 3.4. In words: \(C_{16}\) tells how much normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) a unit of the shear \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) causes, \(C_{61}\) how much shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) a unit of the stretch \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) causes, and the symmetry requires these two cross effects to be equal. The symmetry does not come from the symmetry of stress or strain, but from the requirement that the material does not deliver work in a cycle. Our imagined material with \(C_{16} = 10\) GPa and \(C_{61} = 0\) does not satisfy it, so no such material exists. In figure 3.138 the works along the first and the second path to the strain \(C\) with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = a\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = b\) are \(\tfrac12 C_{11}\,a^2 + \tfrac12 C_{66}\,b^2 + C_{61}\,a\,b\) and \(\tfrac12 C_{11}\,a^2 + \tfrac12 C_{66}\,b^2 + C_{16}\,a\,b\), and with a symmetric matrix they are equal. The proof tells us a little more. Steps 3 and 4 did not need linearity, only continuous mixed derivatives. For a nonlinear ideal elastic material, too, the derivative of the stress \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\) with respect to the component \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}\) therefore equals the derivative of the stress \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{q}}\) with respect to the component \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\), whenever these derivatives are continuous (SADD (6.1.13), PDF p. 132).

Formula (3.70) generalizes \(\tfrac12\,\sigma\,\varepsilon\) of the bar. The half has the same origin, shown in figure 3.143, right: along the straight path all stresses grow evenly from zero to their final values, so each is on average half its final value, and the triangle under the line has half the area of the rectangle. The formula holds only for linear materials, because the even growth entered step 2 of the proof through linearity. In a nonlinear material the stresses do not grow evenly along the straight path, and \(w\) is not half the sum of the products. If the only stress grew with the square of the parameter, as \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,t^2\) (the grey curve), the area under it would be \(\int_0^1 t^2\,\mathrm{d}t = \tfrac13\) of the final value, because the function \(t^3/3\) has the derivative \(t^2\). The energy density would be a third of the product of stress and strain, not a half, so a third smaller than the formula gives. We will see the curves of real materials in figure 3.152.

3.6.6 Change of volume and change of shape

Let us apply formula (3.70) to an isotropic material. By Hooke's law (3.28) its stresses are

\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} , & \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} &= \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} , & \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} &= \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} , & \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} &= 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} , & \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} &= 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} , \end{aligned}\]

where \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) are the Lamé constants, \(\mu\) is the shear modulus \(G\), and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is the volumetric strain, which for small strains gives the relative change of volume of a small piece (section 1.17).

  1. By equation (3.70), \(w = \tfrac12\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} + 2\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}})\), where each shear pair is written once with a factor two.
  2. We insert the stresses. The terms with \(\lambda\) give \(\lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}) = \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2\). The terms with \(\mu\) give \(2\mu\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}^2) + 2 \cdot 2\mu\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}^2)\).
  3. We multiply by \(\tfrac12\):
\[\begin{aligned} w &= \tfrac12\,\lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 + \mu\,\big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}^2 + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}^2 + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}^2\big) \\ &= \tfrac12\,\lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 + \mu \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 . \end{aligned} \tag{3.71}\]
\[w = \tfrac12\,\lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ll}} + \mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} . \tag{3.71}\]

SADD (6.1.9) (PDF p. 131) and EP (3.2.16) (p. 107) write it this way, the latter also with a term for temperature, which we add in section 3.6.8. Let us check lemma 3.61 on the stress as the derivative of the energy density. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\) is a sum in which \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) appears with the factor one, the partial derivative of \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2\) with respect to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is \(2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\), so \(\partial w/\partial\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The line of the steel in figure 3.146 says the same: its height is the derivative of the energy \(w_{\mathrm{V}} = \tfrac12\,K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2\) with respect to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\), and the area under it is the energy itself. We write the shear term with the engineering shear strain, \(2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 = \tfrac12\,\mu\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2\), and its derivative with respect to \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is \(\mu\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). Hooke's law for an isotropic material therefore has an energy density, as it must.

Formula (3.71) can be written differently, so that it shows how much energy goes into the change of volume and how much into the change of shape. Let us first draw what these two changes are, on the piece from the tension test (figure 3.144, top row).

From steel with \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\), which we stretch in the direction \(x\) by \(\varepsilon = 0{,}001\), let us cut a small cube with the edge \(h = 10\) mm and look at it from the front, in the \(xy\) plane. The loaded cube has its edge in the direction \(x\) longer by \(0{,}001 \cdot 10\) mm \(= 10\) µm, and its lateral edges shorter by \(\nu \cdot 10\) µm \(= 3\) µm. In the figure all changes are five hundred times too large, otherwise we would not see them. We write this strain as a sum of two. The first part lengthens all edges equally, each by \(1{,}33\) µm: the cube stays a cube, only its volume changes. The second part lengthens the edge in the direction \(x\) by \(8{,}67\) µm and shortens the lateral edges by \(4{,}33\) µm, exactly as much as keeps the volume the same: only the shape changes. The sum of the two is the true strain, \(1{,}33 + 8{,}67 = 10\) µm along and \(1{,}33 - 4{,}33 = -3\) µm across.

Where do these two numbers come from? The first part stretches the piece equally in all directions, by a third of the volumetric strain, \(\tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\). The second part is what remains: the deviatoric strain of definition 2.114, which in section 3.2.11 we connected with the stress deviator, with the components

\[\begin{aligned} e_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} - \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} , & e_{\mathrm{yy}} &= \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} - \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} , & e_{\mathrm{zz}} &= \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} - \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} , \\ e_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} , & e_{\mathrm{xz}} &= \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} , & e_{\mathrm{yz}} &= \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} . \end{aligned}\]

Its volumetric strain is \(e_{\mathrm{xx}} + e_{\mathrm{yy}} + e_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\), so it does not change the volume. For our cube \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0{,}001 - 2 \cdot 0{,}0003 = 0{,}0004\). A third of this is \(0{,}000133\), which on an edge of 10 mm is \(1{,}33\) µm, and \(e_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}001 - 0{,}000133 = 0{,}000867\), which is \(8{,}67\) µm. The split holds for every small strain, not only for tension. With it we rearrange the sum of squares.

  1. The sum of squares in equation (3.71) has a normal part \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}^2\) and a shear part. The shear part is the same for the components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and for the components \(e_{\mathrm{ij}}\), because their shear components are equal: the deviatoric part of the cube turns the edges only in shear, as the whole strain does.
  2. In the normal part we insert \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = e_{\mathrm{xx}} + \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\) and expand the square: \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 = e_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + \tfrac23\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,e_{\mathrm{xx}} + \tfrac19\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2\). Likewise for \(y\) and \(z\).
  3. We add up. The middle terms give \(\tfrac23\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\,(e_{\mathrm{xx}} + e_{\mathrm{yy}} + e_{\mathrm{zz}}) = 0\), because the deviatoric part does not change the volume. The last terms give \(3 \cdot \tfrac19\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 = \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2\). Hence \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 + \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2\).
  4. We insert this into equation (3.71): \(w = \tfrac12\,\lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 + \tfrac13\,\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 + \mu \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 = \tfrac12\,(\lambda + \tfrac23\,\mu)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 + \mu \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2\).
  5. The number \(\lambda + \tfrac23\,\mu\) is the bulk modulus \(K = E/\big(3\,(1 - 2\nu)\big)\) (definition 3.15). Indeed, by definition 3.18, \(\lambda = E\nu/\big((1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)\big)\) and \(\mu = E/\big(2\,(1 + \nu)\big)\), so
    \[\lambda + \tfrac23\,\mu = \frac{3E\nu + E\,(1 - 2\nu)}{3\,(1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)} = \frac{E\,(1 + \nu)}{3\,(1 + \nu)(1 - 2\nu)} = \frac{E}{3\,(1 - 2\nu)} = K .\]
  6. Hence
\[w = \tfrac12\,K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 + G \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 . \tag{3.72}\]
\[w = \tfrac12\,K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ll}} + G\,e_{\mathrm{ij}}\,e_{\mathrm{ij}} . \tag{3.72}\]

The first term is the volumetric part of the energy density (prostorninski del), which we denote by \(w_{\mathrm{V}}\), the second the distortional part (del zaradi spremembe oblike), which we denote by \(w_{\mathrm{D}}\) (SADD (6.1.15)-(6.1.17), PDF p. 132):

\[w = w_{\mathrm{V}} + w_{\mathrm{D}} , \qquad w_{\mathrm{V}} = \tfrac12\,K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 , \qquad w_{\mathrm{D}} = G \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 .\]

A strain that changes only the volume, as in the cube under even pressure in the bottom row of figure 3.144, has all components \(e_{\mathrm{ij}}\) equal to zero and stores only \(w_{\mathrm{V}}\), which the bulk modulus governs. A strain that changes only the shape, like the shear, has \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\) and stores only \(w_{\mathrm{D}}\), which the shear modulus governs. There is no term that contains both parts at once. In an isotropic material the change of volume and the change of shape are independent in energy, like two springs that we stretch each on its own. This agrees with the fact that in an isotropic material an even pressure changes only the volume and the deviatoric part of stress only the shape (SADD, PDF p. 132). In the lectures the energy density is \(U\), its parts are \(U_{\mathrm{V}}\) and \(U_{\mathrm{D}}\), the deviatoric part of the strain is \(\varepsilon^D_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and the volumetric strain is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}}\) or \(e\) (with us \(e_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is the deviatoric part). In place of \(K\) the lectures have \((2\mu + 3\lambda)/3\), which by step 5 is the same number.

How much energy goes into the change of volume in a tension test? Take the cube of the top row of figure 3.144, steel at a strain of \(\varepsilon = 0{,}001\) in the direction \(x\), with \(E = 196\) GPa and Poisson's ratio \(\nu = 0{,}3\) (definition 3.8). The lateral strains are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nu\,\varepsilon = -0{,}0003\), and there are no shear strains.

  1. The volumetric strain is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = \varepsilon - 2\nu\,\varepsilon = (1 - 2\nu)\,\varepsilon = 0{,}4 \cdot 0{,}001 = 0{,}0004\). A third of it, \(0{,}000133\), is the stretch of the first part in every direction.
  2. The components of the deviatoric part are \(e_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon - \tfrac13\,(1 - 2\nu)\,\varepsilon = \tfrac23\,(1 + \nu)\,\varepsilon = 0{,}000867\) and \(e_{\mathrm{yy}} = e_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nu\,\varepsilon - \tfrac13\,(1 - 2\nu)\,\varepsilon = -\tfrac13\,(1 + \nu)\,\varepsilon = -0{,}000433\). The sum of their squares is \((\tfrac49 + \tfrac19 + \tfrac19)\,(1 + \nu)^2\,\varepsilon^2 = \tfrac23\,(1 + \nu)^2\,\varepsilon^2 = 1{,}1267 \cdot 10^{-6}\).
  3. With \(K = E/\big(3\,(1 - 2\nu)\big)\) the volumetric part is
    \[\begin{aligned} \tfrac12\,K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 &= \frac12 \cdot \frac{E}{3\,(1 - 2\nu)} \cdot (1 - 2\nu)^2\,\varepsilon^2 = \frac{1 - 2\nu}{3} \cdot \tfrac12 E\,\varepsilon^2 \\ &= \frac{0{,}4}{3} \cdot 98\,000\ \text{J/m}^3 = 13\,067\ \text{J/m}^3 . \end{aligned}\]
  4. With \(G = E/\big(2\,(1 + \nu)\big)\) the distortional part is
    \[\begin{aligned} G \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 &= \frac{E}{2\,(1 + \nu)} \cdot \tfrac23\,(1 + \nu)^2\,\varepsilon^2 = \frac{2\,(1 + \nu)}{3} \cdot \tfrac12 E\,\varepsilon^2 \\ &= \frac{2{,}6}{3} \cdot 98\,000\ \text{J/m}^3 = 84\,933\ \text{J/m}^3 . \end{aligned}\]

The shares \((1 - 2\nu)/3\) and \(2\,(1 + \nu)/3\) add up to \((1 - 2\nu + 2 + 2\nu)/3 = 1\), so the sum is \(98\,000\) J/m³, as we computed with the formula \(\tfrac12 E\,\varepsilon^2\). Only 13,3 % of the energy goes into the change of volume, 86,7 % into the change of shape. Why so little into the volume? Because the piece gets thinner, the lateral strains eat up \(2\nu = 60\) % of the stretch, and the volume changes only by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0{,}4\,\varepsilon\). A material with Poisson's ratio close to \(0{,}5\), like rubber, hardly changes its volume, the share \((1 - 2\nu)/3\) is almost zero, and almost all the energy goes into the change of shape (section 3.6.7).

The bottom row of figure 3.144 shows two pure cases. In the pure shear of the cube of section 2.6.6, with the shear stress \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa between the faces \(x\) and \(z\), which we look at in the \(xz\) plane, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\), and the only nonzero strain component is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tau_0/(2G) = 3{,}3163 \cdot 10^{-4}\), with \(G = E/\big(2\,(1 + \nu)\big) = 196/2{,}6\) GPa \(= 75{,}38\) GPa. The cube shears: each of its sides turns by the angle \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}000332\), the right angle between them decreases by twice as much, and for small strains the lengths of the edges do not change. All the energy goes into the change of shape, \(w = G \cdot 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}^2 = \tau_0\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 50 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa} \cdot 3{,}3163 \cdot 10^{-4} = 16\,582\) J/m³, because \(2G\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tau_0\). This is the bar below the sheared cube.

Under the even pressure \(p = 100\) MPa, on the other hand, all components \(e_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are zero. With \(K = E/\big(3\,(1 - 2\nu)\big) = 196/1{,}2\) GPa \(= 163{,}3\) GPa the volumetric strain is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = -p/K = -6{,}12 \cdot 10^{-4}\). The cube shrinks and stays a cube, each edge gets shorter by a third of this, by \(2{,}04\) µm. All the energy goes into the change of volume, \(w = \tfrac12\,K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 = p^2/(2K) = 30\,612\) J/m³, which is the bar below the compressed cube.

The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2\) has nine terms. Can we measure the change of shape with a single number? For the stress we already found such a number in chapter 2: the octahedral shear stress \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}\) (definition 2.109, lemma 2.110). Let us draw it and see what it does to the material (figure 3.145).

The principal axes of stress \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\) and \(\vek e_3\) are the directions in which only a normal stress acts on the faces. The octahedral plane is equally inclined to all three, so its normal \(\vek n\) has all three components equally large. The stress on this plane has a normal part, the mean stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\), and a shear part that lies in the plane, the octahedral shear stress \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}\). Now imagine at the plane a small square piece, which we look at from the side, so that one of its sides lies in the direction \(t\) of the shear stress and the other in the direction of the normal. On its faces acts the shear stress \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}\). The material is isotropic, so Hooke's law holds in every rectangular Cartesian coordinate system with the same two constants (assumption 3 in section 3.2.1), also in the one with the axes \(t\) and \(\vek n\). The shear stress \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}\) therefore shears the piece as in pure shear (lemma 3.16): the right angle between the sides decreases by \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}/G\), and each side turns by half of this angle. The normal stresses on the piece change the lengths of the sides, not the angle between them. We give the half angle a name.

Lemma 3.63 Distortional energy by one quantity (energija spremembe oblike z eno količino)

Let the material at the point \(P\) be ideal elastic, linear elastic and isotropic, with the shear modulus \(G > 0\). Let a small strain be given at \(P\), with the deviatoric part with components \(e_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and let \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}\) be the octahedral shear stress, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\) the von Mises equivalent stress and \(J_2\) the second invariant of the stress deviator that belong to this strain by Hooke's law. The number

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}} = \frac{\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}}{2G} \tag{3.73}\]

is called the octahedral shear strain (oktaedrska strižna deformacija). Then

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}} = \sqrt{\tfrac13 \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2} ,\]

and the distortional part of the strain energy density is

\[w_{\mathrm{D}} = G \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 = 3G\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}^2 = \frac{3\,\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}^2}{4G} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2}{6G} = \frac{J_2}{2G} . \tag{3.74}\]
Proof

All the equalities follow from the relation between the deviatoric parts of stress and strain. The quantities are shown in figure 3.145.

  1. The deviatoric part of stress in an isotropic material is \(s_{\mathrm{ij}} = 2G\,e_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (equation (3.29)). We square and add over all nine pairs of indices:
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} s_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 = 4G^2 \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 .\]
  2. By equation (2.105), \(J_2 = \tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} s_{\mathrm{ij}}^2\), so \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 = 2J_2/(4G^2) = J_2/(2G^2)\). We multiply by \(G\):
    \[w_{\mathrm{D}} = G \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 = \frac{J_2}{2G} .\]
  3. By lemma 2.110 the octahedral shear stress is \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}} = \sqrt{\tfrac23\,J_2}\), hence \(J_2 = \tfrac32\,\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}^2\) and
    \[w_{\mathrm{D}} = \frac{3\,\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}^2}{4G} .\]
  4. We insert \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}} = 2G\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}\) from (3.73), where \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}\) is the angle by which a side of the piece turns:
    \[w_{\mathrm{D}} = \frac{3 \cdot 4G^2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}^2}{4G} = 3G\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}^2 .\]
  5. By definition 2.107, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt{3 J_2}\), hence \(J_2 = \tfrac13\,\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2\), and from step 2 follows
    \[w_{\mathrm{D}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2}{6G} .\]
  6. From steps 2 and 4, \(G \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 = 3G\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}^2\). We divide by \(3G\), which is not zero, and get \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}^2 = \tfrac13 \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2\). Since \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}} \ge 0\) and \(G > 0\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}} \ge 0\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}\) is the nonnegative root of the right side.

Source: The split of the energy and \(w_{\mathrm{D}}\) expressed with the differences of stresses: SADD (6.1.15)-(6.1.17) (PDF p. 132). That the distortional energy is connected with the octahedral shear stress, SADD states without a derivation (PDF pp. 73 and 133). The derivation here uses equation (3.29) and lemma 2.110.

The lemma says that the change of shape has a single measure in the energy. Two states with the same \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}\) store the same distortional energy, even if one is tension and the other shear. Let us check it on both examples. In the tension test of steel at \(\varepsilon = 0{,}001\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sigma = 196\) MPa, so \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}} = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{3} \cdot 196\) MPa \(= 92{,}4\) MPa and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}} = 92{,}4\ \text{MPa}/(2 \cdot 75{,}38\ \text{GPa}) = 0{,}000613\). Then

\[\begin{aligned} w_{\mathrm{D}} &= 3G\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}^2 = 3 \cdot 75{,}385 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa} \cdot (6{,}1283 \cdot 10^{-4})^2 = 84\,933\ \text{J/m}^3 , \\ w_{\mathrm{D}} &= \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}^2}{6G} = \frac{(196 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa})^2}{6 \cdot 75{,}385 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa}} = 84\,933\ \text{J/m}^3 , \end{aligned}\]

which is the bar below the second part in figure 3.144. The deviatoric part of the strain gives the same \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}\) directly: \(\sqrt{\tfrac13 \cdot \tfrac23\,(1 + \nu)^2\,\varepsilon^2} = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{3} \cdot 1{,}3 \cdot 0{,}001 = 0{,}000613\). In pure shear with \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa, \(J_2 = \tau_0^2\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sqrt3\,\tau_0 = 86{,}6\) MPa, \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}} = \sqrt{\tfrac23}\,\tau_0 = 40{,}8\) MPa, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}} = 0{,}000271\) and \(w_{\mathrm{D}} = 3G\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}^2 = 16\,582\) J/m³, which is the bar below the sheared cube. The octahedral shear strain is here smaller than the turn of the sides \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}000332\), because the octahedral plane is not the plane of the largest shear: \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}} = \sqrt{\tfrac23}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\).

In the lectures the octahedral shear strain is \(\varepsilon^{okt}_\gamma\) and equation (3.74) reads \(U_{\mathrm{D}} = 3\mu\,(\varepsilon^{okt}_\gamma)^2\). Because this one quantity determines the distortional energy, we say that the octahedral shear strain measures the change of shape of a body.

The criterion that predicts the onset of yield when \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\) reaches the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) therefore says that the material starts to yield when the distortional energy reaches the value \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}^2/(6G)\), which it has in a tension test at the onset of yield. For steel with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa this is \(107\,007\) J/m³. The condition that \(\tau_{\mathrm{oct}}\) reaches \(\tfrac{\sqrt2}{3}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 103{,}7\) MPa says the same. SADD mentions such criteria (PDF p. 133), and we wrote down the yield condition with the von Mises equivalent stress in section 2.12.6. How the idea arose, the story tells.

From history

When does a material under load in several directions start to yield? James Clerk Maxwell wrote in a letter to his friend Thomson that he had never seen an investigation of the question when a small piece of material gives way, if the strain in three directions is given (TIMO, PDF p. 308). He believed that the piece starts to give way when the energy of change of shape reaches a limit (TIMO, PDF p. 308). He showed that the total energy per unit volume splits into two parts, the energy of uniform tension or compression and the energy of change of shape (TIMO, PDF p. 307). He did not return to the question, and his letters were published only later, in book form in 1937, so his idea was long unknown (TIMO, PDF p. 308).

Beltrami proposed in 1885 that the measure should be all the stored energy per unit volume (TIMO, PDF p. 308). Experiments did not confirm this, because under uniform pressure a large energy is stored without the material yielding or breaking (TIMO, PDF p. 308). In our example, in a tension test of steel only 13,3 % of the energy goes to the change of volume, and under uniform pressure all of it, and the shape does not change. Huber in 1904 took only the energy of change of shape, and von Mises independently of him in 1913 (TIMO, PDF p. 308-309). This energy is proportional to the sum of squares of the differences of the principal stresses, that is, to \(J_2\) from (2.106) (TIMO, PDF p. 308).

3.6.7 An incompressible material in the energy

In section 3.2.12 we met the incompressible material as the limit \(\nu = \tfrac12\), at which the bulk modulus \(K\) grows beyond all bounds. In the volumetric part of the energy \(w_{\mathrm{V}} = \tfrac12\,K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2\), \(K\) stands next to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2\): the first grows, the second falls. What happens to the product? Let us draw it as an area (figure 3.146).

Let us compress the cube with the even pressure \(p = 100\) MPa. On the horizontal axis we plot the size of the volumetric strain \(|\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}|\), on the vertical one the size of the mean stress \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{m}}|\). By equation (3.29), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\), which is a line through the origin with the slope \(K\). It reaches the height \(p\) at \(|\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}| = p/K\), and the work of the pressure per unit volume is the area of the triangle below it,

\[w_{\mathrm{V}} = \tfrac12\,p \cdot \frac{p}{K} = \frac{p^2}{2K} .\]

For steel with \(\nu = 0{,}3\), \(K = 163{,}3\) GPa, \(|\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}| = 6{,}12 \cdot 10^{-4}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{V}} = 30\,612\) J/m³, as for the compressed cube in figure 3.144. Now let us change only \(\nu\) and keep the shear modulus \(G = 75{,}38\) GPa, so that the material resists shear as steel does. From \(E = 2G\,(1 + \nu)\) follows \(K = 2G\,(1 + \nu)/\big(3\,(1 - 2\nu)\big)\) (computed with NumPy):

\(\nu\) \(K\) [GPa] \(\lvert\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\rvert = p/K\) \(w_{\mathrm{V}} = p^2/(2K)\) [J/m³]
0,3 163,3 \(6{,}12 \cdot 10^{-4}\) 30 612
0,45 728,7 \(1{,}37 \cdot 10^{-4}\) 6 861
0,49 3 744 \(0{,}27 \cdot 10^{-4}\) 1 335
0,4999 376 898 \(0{,}0027 \cdot 10^{-4}\) 13

At \(\nu = 0{,}45\) and \(\nu = 0{,}49\), the value of rubber, the line is ever steeper and the triangle ever narrower, while the height stays \(p\). As \(K\) grows beyond all bounds, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = -p/K\) goes to zero and with it \(w_{\mathrm{V}} = p^2/(2K)\). In the product \(\tfrac12\,K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2\) falls as \(1/K^2\), faster than \(K\) grows. In the limit the line is the vertical axis, and there is no triangle left. For an incompressible material (nestisljiv material), therefore, under every load

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0 , \qquad w_{\mathrm{V}} = 0 , \qquad w = w_{\mathrm{D}} = G \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 ,\]

where in the last equation we used that at \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\) the deviatoric part is the strain itself, \(e_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Pressure does no work in an incompressible material, because nothing moves under it. The price is that we can no longer compute the mean stress from the strain: in \(\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\) stands infinity times zero. The law of the material then determines only the deviatoric part of the stress, and the mean stress is determined by the equations of equilibrium and the boundary conditions (BOWER §3.5.4, PDF p. 127). In the lectures the same is written as \(U_{\mathrm{V}} = 0\) and \(e = \varepsilon_{11} + \varepsilon_{22} + \varepsilon_{33} = 0\).

Incompressibility is an idealization, so let us say when we may take it and what it costs.

  • Why it makes sense: rubber has \(\nu = 0{,}49\) (BOWER, table 3.1, PDF p. 100), its triangle is twenty-three times narrower than that of steel. BOWER says that most rubbers strongly resist a change of volume and that in hand calculations it is sometimes convenient to treat them as perfectly incompressible (BOWER §3.5.4, PDF p. 126).
  • When it holds: under loads that change the shape, such as tension, shear and bending. It does not hold when the load is almost pure pressure, because then the small change of volume is the only strain that is left at all. Nor does it hold for fast events: in an incompressible material the speed of pressure waves would be infinite (BOWER §3.5.4, PDF p. 127).
  • What it does to the result: in a tension test we leave out the share \((1 - 2\nu)/3\) of the energy. For rubber with \(\nu = 0{,}49\) this is \(0{,}67\) %, for steel with \(\nu = 0{,}3\) it is \(13{,}3\) %, the blue bar in figure 3.144. Steel must therefore not be treated as incompressible.

3.6.8 Energy with temperature

So far the material was at the reference temperature all the time. What is the energy density if the material is heated by \(\Delta T\)? By Hooke's law with temperature (theorem 3.23) only the elastic part of the strain causes stress, while we measure the whole strain, together with the thermal one. The answer therefore depends on what we mean by the word energy. Three quantities are possible, which are equal at \(\Delta T = 0\) but not in a heated material. Let us first draw them for a bar, where all three are areas on the same graph (figure 3.147).

Take the steel bar of section 3.3.3, with \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\alpha = 15 \cdot 10^{-6}\) 1/K, heated by \(\Delta T = 30\) K. Its lateral surface is free, so the only stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), and by the first equation of (3.31), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E + \alpha\,\Delta T\). On the axes are the total strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The unheated bar has a line through the origin with the slope \(E\). The heated bar has the line \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} - \alpha\,\Delta T)\) with the same slope, shifted to the right by \(\alpha\,\Delta T = 0{,}00045\). At the point \(B\) the bar is freely heated: longer and without stress. At the point \(A\) the bar is between the walls of equation (3.36): \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -88{,}2\) MPa. At the point \(C\) we have also pulled the heated bar to a total strain of \(0{,}001\), where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 196\ \text{GPa} \cdot (0{,}001 - 0{,}00045) = 107{,}8\) MPa.

  1. The energy of the elastic part of the strain. This is the work that the stress does from the state without stress, the point \(B\), to the given state, that is, the area between the line and the axis, measured from \(B\). At \(C\) this is the triangle with the base \(0{,}001 - 0{,}00045 = 0{,}00055\) and the height \(107{,}8\) MPa, \(\tfrac12 \cdot 107{,}8 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa} \cdot 0{,}00055 = 29\,645\) J/m³. At \(A\) it is the triangle with the base \(0{,}00045\) and the height \(88{,}2\) MPa, \(19\,845\) J/m³. The bar gives this energy back when we release it: the bar between the walls gets longer when a wall is taken away, and does work in the process.
  2. The work of the stress from point \(A\). At a constant temperature we go from \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\), the point \(A\), to \(C\). The work is the area under the line with its sign: negative below the axis, positive above it, \(-19\,845 + 29\,645 = 9\,800\) J/m³. Point \(A\) is not the undeformed shape: the bar is wider there by \(0{,}000585\) across. The work from zero strain in all directions, \(w_{\mathrm{T}}\) in the table below, is therefore a different number at \(A\) and at \(C\), but their difference is the same \(9\,800\) J/m³. It differs from the energy of the elastic part by the triangle at \(A\), which is the same for all end points.
  3. Half the product of the stress and the total strain. At \(C\), \(\tfrac12\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12 \cdot 107{,}8 \cdot 10^6\ \text{Pa} \cdot 0{,}001 = 53\,900\) J/m³, the triangle with the hypotenuse from the origin to \(C\). This triangle is not an area under the line of the material, because the line of the heated bar passes through \(B\) and not through the origin. At \(A\) this quantity is \(\tfrac12 \cdot (-88{,}2\ \text{MPa}) \cdot 0 = 0\), although the bar is compressed.

Now the same for a general state, where the temperature shifts the line as for the bar. In section 3.3.2 we split Hooke's law with temperature into the volumetric and the deviatoric part (equation (3.35)):

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{m}} = K\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} - 3\alpha\,\Delta T) , \qquad s_{\mathrm{ij}} = 2G\,e_{\mathrm{ij}} .\]

The temperature term is the same in all three equations for the normal stresses and absent from the shear ones, so only the mean stress has it.

Heating therefore shifts only the line of the mean stress, by \(3\alpha\,\Delta T\) to the right, as in figure 3.147 it shifted the line of the bar by \(\alpha\,\Delta T\). For our steel \(3K\,\alpha\,\Delta T = 3 \cdot 163{,}3\ \text{GPa} \cdot 0{,}00045 = 220{,}5\) MPa. The distortional part does not change, in all three quantities it is \(w_{\mathrm{D}} = G \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 = 3G\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{oct}}^2\) of lemma 3.63. They differ only in the volumetric part.

The form of the source. The source uses the orange triangle of the figure. For an isotropic linear elastic material with a change of temperature \(\Delta T\), EP writes (EP (3.2.16), p. 107, with the stresses of EP (3.2.13), which are our equations (3.32))

\[U_0 = \frac12\Big[2\mu \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 + \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 - \alpha\,(2\mu + 3\lambda)\,\Delta T\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\Big] . \tag{3.75}\]
\[U_0 = \frac12\big[2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} + \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ii}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jj}} - \alpha\,(2\mu + 3\lambda)\,\Delta T\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{jj}}\big] . \tag{3.75}\]

This is the orange triangle, \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\), with the stresses of the heated material and with the total strain, that is, quantity 3. With the split \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 + \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2\) and with \(2\mu + 3\lambda = 3K\) we get (checked with SymPy)

\[U_0 = G \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 + \tfrac12\,K\,\big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 - 3\alpha\,\Delta T\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\big) .\]

The line of the lectures. In the lectures the orange triangle is \(U = \tfrac12\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) with the total strain and with the stresses with the temperature term, which gives \(U = \mu\,\varepsilon^D_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon^D_{\mathrm{ij}} + \tfrac{2\mu + 3\lambda}{6}\,\big(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}}^2 - 3\alpha\,T\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}}\big)\), where \(T\) means our \(\Delta T\). Since \((2\mu + 3\lambda)/6 = K/2\), this is the same equation as \(U_0\) of the source. The source and the lectures therefore do not differ. In parts, \(U_{\mathrm{D}} = 3\mu\,(\varepsilon^{okt}_\gamma)^2\) and \(U_{\mathrm{V}} = \tfrac{2\mu + 3\lambda}{6}\,(e^2 - 3\alpha\,T\,e)\).

How both differ from the work of the stress. We defined the strain energy density as the work of the stress (definition 3.59), and EP defines it so too (EP (3.2.5), p. 103, and (3.2.7), p. 106). Let us compute this work for a heated material as the area under the line in figure 3.148, from zero strain to the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at a constant \(\Delta T\).

  1. We go along a straight path to the final strain, on which at the parameter \(t\) between \(0\) and \(1\) all strain components are \(t\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The stress is then \(t\,\sigma^0_{\mathrm{ij}}\) plus a constant temperature part: \(-3K\,\alpha\,\Delta T\) in all three normal stresses. Here \(\sigma^0_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the stresses that Hooke's law without temperature gives for the final strain.
  2. The first part grows from zero in proportion to the strain, like the line through the origin. Its work is a triangle, \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma^0_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\), which by equation (3.72) equals \(\tfrac12\,K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 + G \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2\).
  3. The second part is the same all the time, so its work is a rectangle and not a triangle: the stress \(-3K\,\alpha\,\Delta T\) times the sum of the three normal strains, \(-3K\,\alpha\,\Delta T\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\), without the half.
  4. We add up the triangle and the rectangle:
    \[w_{\mathrm{T}} = G \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 + \tfrac12\,K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 - 3K\,\alpha\,\Delta T\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} . \tag{3.76}\]

The work does not depend on the path: the first part, the triangle, is the work of the material without temperature, which is ideal elastic, and the work of a constant stress, the rectangle, depends only on the final \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\). The temperature term in \(w_{\mathrm{T}}\) is twice as large as in \(U_0\). The half belongs only to the part of the stress that grows from zero. The difference shows in differentiation. The derivative of \(w_{\mathrm{T}}\) with respect to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), as lemma 3.61 requires (EP (3.2.6), p. 103). The derivative of \(U_0\) with respect to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), however, is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \tfrac32\,K\,\alpha\,\Delta T\) (both checked with SymPy), for our steel \(110{,}25\) MPa too much. From \(U_0\), therefore, at \(\Delta T \ne 0\) we do not get the stresses by differentiation.

The energy of the elastic part of the strain, quantity 1, which in figure 3.147 is the blue triangles, follows from the picture of two steps in section 3.3.2. The second step is the ordinary loading of a material without stress, and its strain is the elastic part, which has the volumetric strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} - 3\alpha\,\Delta T\) and the same deviatoric part. By equation (3.72),

\[w_{\mathrm{el}} = G \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 + \tfrac12\,K\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} - 3\alpha\,\Delta T)^2 = w_{\mathrm{T}} + \tfrac92\,K\,\alpha^2\,\Delta T^2 . \tag{3.77}\]

The second equality follows when we expand the square. \(w_{\mathrm{el}}\) differs from \(w_{\mathrm{T}}\) by a number that does not depend on the strain, so they have the same derivatives. For our steel \(\tfrac92\,K\,\alpha^2\,\Delta T^2 = 148\,838\) J/m³: this much energy has a cube whose expansion we prevent completely when it is heated by 30 K, so that the pressure in it is \(220{,}5\) MPa. The table collects all three quantities for four states of the heated steel (in J/m³, computed with NumPy).

state \(U_0 = \tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (source, lectures) \(w_{\mathrm{T}}\) (work of the stress) \(w_{\mathrm{el}}\) (elastic part)
freely heated, point \(B\) 0 −148 838 0
bar between walls, point \(A\) 0 −128 993 19 845
heated and pulled bar, point \(C\) 53 900 −119 193 29 645
cube that cannot expand in any direction 0 0 148 838

In every row \(w_{\mathrm{el}} - w_{\mathrm{T}} = 148\,838\) J/m³, and between the points \(A\) and \(C\) \(w_{\mathrm{T}}\) increases by \(9\,800\) J/m³, as we computed on the graph. Which quantity should we take, then?

  • At \(\Delta T = 0\) the line of the heated bar coincides with the unheated one and all three are equal, and everything we derived in this section before temperature holds unchanged.
  • For the energy that the material can give back we take \(w_{\mathrm{el}}\), the blue triangles. It is the only one of the three that is zero exactly when there is no stress.
  • For the stresses, the heights of the line, as derivatives of the energy we take \(w_{\mathrm{T}}\) or \(w_{\mathrm{el}}\), which have the same derivatives.
  • Equation (3.75) of the source and the lectures is half the product of the stress and the total strain. It does not measure the stored energy: at the points \(A\) and \(B\) it is zero, although the bar at \(A\) is compressed. At the point \(C\) it counts the thermal strain as if the stress had caused it, and gives \(53\,900\) J/m³ instead of \(29\,645\) J/m³.

For \(w_{\mathrm{el}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{T}}\) we assumed the same as for Hooke's law with temperature: the constants \(E\), \(\nu\) and \(\alpha\) do not depend on the temperature and the temperature does not change during loading. The first holds for moderate changes of temperature, the second for slow loading, when the heat is exchanged with the surroundings as it arises (section 3.3.2, assumptions 2 and 4). If \(E\) of the heated steel were different, the slope of the line would change and with it all three areas.

3.6.9 Bounds on the elastic constants

Can the elastic constants be any numbers? In the bar, a positive Young's modulus meant that stretching takes pulling and doing work. A material with \(w < 0\) at some strain would give off work when deformed in that way, and it would deform by itself, without a force. A material with \(w = 0\) at a nonzero strain would deform in that way without any resistance. From a stable material we therefore require \(w > 0\) at every small strain that is not zero (SADD (6.1.11), PDF p. 131, where this property is stated for all elastic materials, BOWER, PDF p. 102). This is an assumption about the material, not a consequence of the previous theorems. Why may we assume it? A piece of steel or rubber lying on a table stays as it is. If some small strain lowered its energy, it would take that strain by itself. When does it hold? For small strains of the material from the state without stress. It says nothing about a whole structure: a slender compressed bar can buckle (section 3.3.3), although its material is stable. What does it give? Without it Hooke's law allows every \(E \ne 0\) and every \(\nu\) except \(-1\) and \(\tfrac12\). With it we get the bounds of the next theorem, and for numbers just outside them we shall see in figure 3.149 what would go wrong. What, then, does it say about the constants of an isotropic material?

Theorem 3.64 Bounds on the elastic constants (meje elastičnih konstant)

Let the material be ideal elastic, linear elastic and isotropic, with Young's modulus \(E\) and Poisson's ratio \(\nu\), where \(\nu \ne -1\) and \(\nu \ne \tfrac12\), and let \(K = E/\big(3\,(1 - 2\nu)\big)\) be its bulk modulus and \(G = E/\big(2\,(1 + \nu)\big)\) its shear modulus. Then the following three statements are equivalent, as figure 3.150 shows in the band of admissible \(\nu\):

  1. the strain energy density, the sum of the volumetric and the shape part, is positive, \(w > 0\), at every small strain that is not zero,
  2. \(K > 0\) and \(G > 0\),
  3. \(E > 0\) and \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\).
Proof

We must show that statement 2 follows from statement 1 and conversely, and that statement 3 follows from statement 2 and conversely. We use equation (3.72), \(w = \tfrac12\,K\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^2 + G \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2\). The first term is the volumetric one, the second the shape one.

From 1 follows 2.

  1. Take a strain that changes only the volume: \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = c\), where \(c \ne 0\) is a small number, with no shear components. This is the cube under pressure of figure 3.144, except that each edge \(h\) changes by \(c\,h\) instead of by \(-2{,}04\) µm. Then \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 3c\) and \(e_{\mathrm{xx}} = c - c = 0\), likewise \(e_{\mathrm{yy}} = e_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\), so \(w = \tfrac12\,K \cdot 9c^2\).
  2. By statement 1, \(w > 0\), and since \(\tfrac92\,c^2 > 0\), \(K > 0\).
  3. Take a strain that changes only the shape: \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = c \ne 0\), all other components zero. This is the shear of the same figure, only in the \(xy\) plane, in which each side turns by the angle \(c\). Then \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\), so \(e_{\mathrm{ij}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) for all indices and \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 = c^2 + c^2 = 2c^2\), and \(w = 2\,G\,c^2\).
  4. By statement 1, \(w > 0\), so \(G > 0\).

From 2 follows 1.

  1. Let \(K > 0\) and \(G > 0\). Then both terms of \(w\), the volumetric and the distortional part, are nonnegative, so \(w \ge 0\).
  2. Let \(w = 0\). A sum of two nonnegative terms, the volumetric and the shape one, is zero only if both are zero, so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = 0\) and \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} e_{\mathrm{ij}}^2 = 0\). A sum of squares is zero only if every square is zero, so all components \(e_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are zero.
  3. The strain is the sum of the volumetric and the shape strain. From \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = e_{\mathrm{xx}} + \tfrac13\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = e_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and the same relations for the other components it follows that the strain is zero.
  4. At a strain that is not zero, therefore, \(w = 0\) is impossible (both terms are not zero), and by step 1 \(w > 0\).

From 3 follows 2.

  1. Let \(E > 0\) and \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\). Then \(1 + \nu > 0\) and \(1 - 2\nu > 0\). In figure 3.150, \(\nu\) lies in the band to the right of the bound \(-1\) and to the left of the bound \(\tfrac12\).
  2. The numerator and the denominator of \(G = E/\big(2\,(1 + \nu)\big)\) are positive, so \(G > 0\). Likewise \(K = E/\big(3\,(1 - 2\nu)\big) > 0\). The curves \(G/E\) and \(K/E\) are above the axis in the band.

From 2 follows 3.

  1. Let \(K > 0\) and \(G > 0\). Since \(G\) is not zero, \(E\) is not zero either, and the reciprocals are \(1/G = 2\,(1 + \nu)/E\) and \(1/K = 3\,(1 - 2\nu)/E\).
  2. We add three times the first and the second. The terms with \(\nu\) cancel:
    \[\frac{3}{G} + \frac{1}{K} = \frac{6 + 6\nu + 3 - 6\nu}{E} = \frac{9}{E} .\]
  3. The left side is positive, so \(E = 9/(3/G + 1/K) > 0\).
  4. From \(G = E/\big(2\,(1 + \nu)\big)\) follows \(1 + \nu = E/(2G) > 0\), so \(\nu > -1\). From \(K = E/\big(3\,(1 - 2\nu)\big)\) follows \(1 - 2\nu = E/(3K) > 0\), so \(\nu < \tfrac12\).

Source: SADD §6.3, (6.3.3), (6.3.6), (6.3.9)-(6.3.11) (PDF pp. 134-135), where the bounds are derived from three stress states: tension, shear and even pressure. BOWER (PDF p. 102) states the bounds for a stable material. The proof through the split into a volumetric and a distortional part is not from the sources.

The proof used two test strains from the bottom row of figure 3.144, and each tests one of the two constants: the cube under pressure the bulk modulus, the shear the shear modulus. Figure 3.150, which extends figure 3.46 beyond both bounds, shows on the axis \(\nu\) what happens at the bounds \(-1\) and \(\tfrac12\), between which lie the admissible values of \(\nu\). As \(\nu\) approaches \(\tfrac12\) from below, \(K/E = 1/\big(3\,(1 - 2\nu)\big)\) grows beyond all bounds: the material resists a change of volume infinitely strongly compared with stretching, it is incompressible, as we said in section 3.2.12. As \(\nu\) approaches \(-1\) from above, \(G/E\) grows beyond all bounds. Above \(\tfrac12\), \(K\) would be negative, below \(-1\), \(G\) would be. For steel with \(\nu = 0{,}3\), \(K/E = 0{,}833\) and \(G/E = 0{,}385\), both positive.

Let us look at two more numbers just outside the bounds, for a material with \(E = 196\) GPa (figure 3.149, where the changes are drawn ten times more enlarged than in figure 3.144). For \(\nu = 0{,}55\), a little above \(\tfrac12\), we have \(1 - 2\nu = -0{,}1\) and

\[K = \frac{E}{3\,(1 - 2\nu)} = \frac{196\ \text{GPa}}{3 \cdot (-0{,}1)} = -653\ \text{GPa} .\]

The bulk modulus is negative. Let us compress a cube with an edge of 10 mm with the even pressure \(p = 100\) MPa. The volumetric strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = -p/K = 1{,}53 \cdot 10^{-4}\) is positive, so the volume would increase, each edge by \(0{,}51\) µm: the pressure would inflate the cube. A steel cube shrinks under the same pressure. For \(\nu = -1{,}1\), a little below \(-1\), we have \(1 + \nu = -0{,}1\) and

\[G = \frac{E}{2\,(1 + \nu)} = \frac{196\ \text{GPa}}{2 \cdot (-0{,}1)} = -980\ \text{GPa} .\]

The shear modulus is negative. The shear stress \(\tau = 50\) MPa would then give a shear \(\gamma = \tau/G = -5{,}1 \cdot 10^{-5}\). Each side would turn by half of this, by \(2{,}55 \cdot 10^{-5}\), and the cube would shear in the direction opposite to the force, unlike the steel one. In both cases statement 2 of the theorem does not hold, so statement 1 does not hold either. The energy density is negative at the strain from the proof: for \(\nu = 0{,}55\) at \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = c\) we have \(w = \tfrac92\,K\,c^2 < 0\), for \(\nu = -1{,}1\) at \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = c\) we have \(w = 2\,G\,c^2 < 0\). In deforming, the material would give off energy instead of receiving it.

The theorem says that Poisson's ratio can also be negative, but larger than \(-1\). Such a material gets wider when stretched, an ordinary one narrower. BOWER mentions that such materials exist (BOWER, PDF p. 102), although most real materials have \(0 < \nu < \tfrac12\) (SADD, PDF p. 135). For an anisotropic material the requirement \(w > 0\) means that the stiffness matrix \(\mat C\) is such that \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{p}}\sum_{\mathrm{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}} > 0\) at every strain that is not zero. One consequence is simple: at a strain whose only nonzero component is \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\), \(w = \tfrac12\,C_{\mathrm{pp}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}^2\) (the parabola), so all diagonal entries \(C_{\mathrm{pp}}\) are positive. The complete conditions, which are written with determinants (section 2.10), are given in SADD (11.3.3) (PDF p. 340). We do not prove them.

3.6.10 Complementary strain energy density

In a uniaxial state the strain energy density is the area under the curve of stress \(\sigma\) against strain \(\varepsilon\), between the curve and the strain axis. The curve from the origin \(O\) splits the rectangle with sides \(\varepsilon_1\) and \(\sigma_1\), the final strain and the final stress, into two parts (figure 3.152). The other part, between the curve and the stress axis, gets a name of its own. In chapter 4 we will need it for methods that look for forces instead of displacements.

From history

Methods of structural analysis that came from energy always assumed that the displacements are linear functions of the forces, and for some structures this does not hold, because the curve of stress against strain bends (TIMO, PDF p. 231). For such cases Friedrich Engesser introduced a new energy quantity in 1889 (TIMO, PDF p. 231).

Let us return to the curve of stress against strain in figure 3.152. Why do the classical methods fail? When the relation between force and displacement is a curve, the strain energy is not a quadratic function of the force, so its derivative with respect to the force does not give the displacement (TIMO, PDF p. 232). Why not, we will draw in figure 3.153. For a linear material the two parts of the rectangle in figure 3.152, left, are equal and the new quantity is not needed. For a curve that is not a straight line, however, they differ. The first part is the strain energy, and the second is the area on the other side of the curve, which Engesser introduced (TIMO, PDF p. 232).

Definition 3.65 Complementary strain energy density (gostota komplementarne energije)

During a loading that starts at the origin \(O\), at zero strain and zero stress, let the strain components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and the stress components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at a point \(P\) change with a parameter \(t\) along the curve from a closed interval \([t_0, t_1]\), and let all these functions be differentiable at every point of the interval \([t_0, t_1]\), at the endpoints with a one-sided derivative (definition 1.9), with derivatives continuous on \([t_0, t_1]\). The complementary strain energy density (gostota komplementarne energije) at \(P\) at the end of the loading is the number

\[w^* = \int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^{t_1} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(t)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}'(t)\,\mathrm{d}t . \tag{3.78}\]

Source: EP (3.2.9) (p. 106) and pp. 103-104 for the uniaxial state, where \(w^* = \int_0^{\sigma} \varepsilon\,\mathrm{d}\sigma\).

The roles are swapped: in \(w\) the stresses work on the changes of strain, in \(w^*\) the strains on the changes of stress. In a uniaxial state we take the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) itself as the parameter, running from \(0\) to \(\sigma_1\), and get \(w^* = \int_0^{\sigma_1} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), the area between the curve and the stress axis (EP, p. 104). How are \(w\) and \(w^*\) related? In a uniaxial state we already see the answer in figure 3.152: the area under the curve and the area along the stress axis together fill the rectangle. For all nine components at once, integration by parts gives the same, in three steps.

  1. For each pair of indices \(i\), \(j\) we use integration by parts (3.56) with the functions \(f = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and \(g = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (corollary 3.56), which in the figure cuts the rectangle into \(w\) and \(w^*\):
    \[\int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^{t_1} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}'\,\mathrm{d}t = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(t_1)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(t_1) - \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(t_0)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(t_0) - \int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^{t_1} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}'\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}t .\]
  2. The loading starts at zero stress, so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(t_0) = 0\), and the middle term drops out. In figure 3.152 this is the origin \(O\), where the curve starts. The assumption holds for a body that is free of stress before loading and whose strain we measure from that shape, as for our bar before the pull. If we counted from a state in which the stress \(\sigma_0\) and the strain \(\varepsilon_0\) are both nonzero, the term would stay, and the corner rectangle \(\sigma_0\,\varepsilon_0\) would be subtracted from the rectangle \(\sigma_1\,\varepsilon_1\).
  3. We move the last integral to the left and add up over all nine pairs of indices. By the linearity of the integral (lemma 3.54, item 1) the left side is the sum of the integral (3.66) and the integral (3.78), the right side the sum of the products of the final stresses and strains, that is, of the areas of rectangles:
    \[\int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^{t_1} \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}'\,\mathrm{d}t + w^* = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(t_1)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(t_1) . \tag{3.79}\]

For an ideal elastic material the first term is the strain energy density \(w\) (definition 3.59), so \(w + w^* = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\), taken at the end of the loading. Since \(w\) and the right side depend only on the final state, so does \(w^*\). In a uniaxial state this is \(w + w^* = \sigma_1\,\varepsilon_1\), the rectangle of figure 3.152.
