For a linear material, by theorem 3.62 on the symmetry of the elastic constants, \(w = \tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\)\(w = \tfrac12\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so also \(w^* = \tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and the two densities are equal, \(w^* = w\). In figure 3.152, left, the line splits the rectangle into two equal triangles, \(w\) and \(w^*\). For the steel bar at the force of 10 kN, with the stress \(127{,}3\) MPa, the strain \(6{,}496 \cdot 10^{-4}\) and \(w = 41\,356\) J/m³, therefore, also \(w^* = 41\,356\) J/m³. Together this is \(82\,711\) J/m³, the area of the rectangle, \(127{,}324\ \text{MPa} \cdot 6{,}496 \cdot 10^{-4}\). They are equal only in value, though. We write \(w\) as a function of the strains and \(w^*\) as a function of the stresses, and in chapter 4 this will matter (EP, p. 107).

For a material whose relation between stress and strain is not a straight line, the two densities differ, and \(w\) is no longer \(\tfrac12\,\sigma_1\,\varepsilon_1\). Rubber is such a material: it sustains large changes of shape and returns to its original shape, but its relation between force and elongation is not a straight line (BOWER §1.1.5, PDF p. 35). The rubber band of section 1.1, stretched by half its length, has such a curve. Its strains, however, are not small, so this example lies outside the model of this section, which works with small strains and with areas and volumes before loading. We cite it only as an example of a curve that is not a straight line. Rubber under large strains is described by hyperelastic models (BOWER §3.5, PDF pp. 120-121). Figure 3.152, right, shows a schematic curve that flattens as the strain grows. The area under it is larger than half the rectangle, in the figure it is 62 % of the rectangle and the area above it 38 %, so \(w > \tfrac12\,\sigma_1\,\varepsilon_1 > w^*\). For a curve that gets steeper as the strain grows it would be the other way round. The stresses are the partial derivatives of the strain energy density with respect to the strains (lemma 3.61). Are, conversely, the strains the partial derivatives of the complementary strain energy density with respect to the stresses, as EP and SADD write (EP, p. 106, SADD (6.6.3), PDF p. 139)? For a linear material and for a uniaxial state with any curve we prove this in the next lemma. For \(w^*\) to be a function of the stresses at all, we need the stresses to determine the strains uniquely.

Why would the strains be derivatives of the density \(w^*\)? Figure 3.153 shows the idea for a uniaxial state, on the axes \(\varepsilon\) and \(\sigma\) with the origin \(O\) and the curve of stress. The density \(w^*\) is the area between the curve and the stress axis up to the stress \(\sigma_1\). When we raise the stress by a small number \(h\), the area grows by a strip of height \(h\) and width \(\varepsilon_1\), the strain at the stress \(\sigma_1\), and by a small piece next to the curve. The increase divided by \(h\) is therefore close to \(\varepsilon_1\). This is the same argument as for the force, which is the derivative of the work with respect to the elongation (section 3.5.7), only with the roles of the axes swapped.

For the steel bar at the force of 10 kN (figure 3.153, right, with the axes from the origin) the curve is a straight line, the stress is \(\sigma_1 = 127{,}3\) MPa and the strain \(\varepsilon_1 = \sigma_1/E = 6{,}496 \cdot 10^{-4}\). When the stress is raised by 1 MPa, the density \(w^* = \sigma^2/(2E)\), the triangle along the stress axis, grows by \(652{,}2\) J/m³, while the strip has the area \(\varepsilon_1 \cdot 1\ \text{MPa} = 649{,}6\) J/m³. The difference of \(2{,}6\) J/m³ comes from the triangle next to the line, \((1\ \text{MPa})^2/(2E)\), which for a smaller step shrinks with the square of the step. The step of 1 MPa is drawn enlarged in the figure, otherwise the strip would be too thin to see.

Why do we not simply differentiate the strain energy density \(w\)? Let us return to the curve on the left. In the same step of stress the strain grows by a number \(k\), and the area under the curve, that is \(w\), grows by an upright strip of height \(\sigma_1\) and width \(k\) and by a small piece under the curve. The upright strip has the area \(\sigma_1\,k\), the lying one the area \(\varepsilon_1\,h\). They are equal only when \(h/k = \sigma_1/\varepsilon_1\), that is when the curve rises during the step as steeply as the straight line from the origin to the point on the curve. For the straight line of the steel bar this holds at every step: the strain grows by \(1\ \text{MPa}/E = 5{,}102 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and the upright strip has the area \(127{,}324\ \text{MPa} \cdot 5{,}102 \cdot 10^{-6} = 649{,}6\) J/m³, the same as the lying one, and the piece under the line the same \(2{,}6\) J/m³. For a linear material, therefore, the derivative of the density \(w\) with respect to the stress also gives the strain. The curve on the left, however, flattens, the strain grows more in an equal step of stress, and the upright strip is in the figure about one half larger than the lying one. The derivative of the density \(w\) with respect to the stress would give too large a strain there. This is why the classical methods fail for a curve, and why Engesser took the area on the other side of the curve.

In compression the picture is the same, only in the third quadrant, where the curve is drawn schematically. The stress \(\sigma_1 = -b\) and the strain \(g(-b)\), a contraction, are negative, while the density \(w^*\) is again the area between the curve and the stress axis, a positive number. The integral of the negative strain from \(-b\) to \(0\) is negative, so in the lemma there will be a minus in front of it for \(\sigma_1 < 0\). For a linear material in several directions \(w^*\) is a quadratic function of the six stress components, and we compute its partial derivatives directly.

Lemma 3.66 Strains as derivatives of the complementary energy density (deformacije kot odvodi gostote komplementarne energije)
  1. Let a material at the point \(P\) be ideal elastic and linear elastic (in the figure the line), with a material stiffness matrix \(\mat C\) that has an inverse \(\mat C^{-1}\). Then at every stress to which a small strain belongs,
    \[w^* = \frac12 \sum_{\mathrm{p}} \sum_{\mathrm{q}} (\mat C^{-1})_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{q}} , \tag{3.80}\]
    where \(p\) and \(q\) run from \(1\) to \(6\), and the partial derivatives of the density \(w^*\) with respect to the six stress components are the strain components:
    \[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{\partial w^*}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} &= \frac{\partial w^*}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}} , & \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} &= \frac{\partial w^*}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}} , \\ \gamma_{\mathrm{yz}} &= \frac{\partial w^*}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}} , & \gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} &= \frac{\partial w^*}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}} , & \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \frac{\partial w^*}{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}} . \end{aligned} \tag{3.81}\]
  2. Let a material at the point \(P\) be ideal elastic and the stress state uniaxial (in the figure the curve of stress against strain), with the only nonzero component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma\). Let \(I\) be an open interval that contains \(0\), and let the strain be small at every stress \(\sigma \in I\), with each of its components a continuously differentiable function of the stress \(\sigma\) on \(I\) that is zero at \(\sigma = 0\). Denote the component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) as a function of the stress by \(g\). Then the complementary strain energy density at the stress \(\sigma_1 \in I\) is
    \[w^*(\sigma_1) = \int_0^{\sigma_1} g(s)\,\mathrm{d}s \quad\text{for } \sigma_1 \ge 0 , \qquad w^*(\sigma_1) = -\int_{\sigma_1}^0 g(s)\,\mathrm{d}s \quad\text{for } \sigma_1 < 0 ,\]
    and \(w^*\) is a differentiable function of the stress with the derivative \(\mathrm{d}w^*/\mathrm{d}\sigma_1 = g(\sigma_1)\), the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) at the stress \(\sigma_1\).
Proof

We have to show both items. In the first we write \(w^*\) with the stresses and differentiate a quadratic function (for a linear material the line). In the second we compute \(w^*\) along a path along the curve on which the parameter is the stress itself, and use the fundamental theorem of calculus.

1. Linear material.

  1. By theorem 3.62 on the symmetry of the elastic constants, \(\mat C\) is symmetric, and by equation (3.70), \(w = \tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{p}} \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\). In the figure \(w\) is the triangle under the line, half of the rectangle.
  2. By (3.79), for an ideal elastic material \(w + w^* = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\), which by (3.67), applied to products, is \(\sum_{\mathrm{p}} \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\). In the figure this is the rectangle that \(w\) and \(w^*\) fill together. With step 1, therefore, \(w^* = \tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{p}} \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\).
  3. By lemma 3.28, \(\{\varepsilon\} = \mat C^{-1}\{\sigma\}\), so \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}} = \sum_{\mathrm{q}} (\mat C^{-1})_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{q}}\). We insert this into step 2 and get (3.80).
  4. The matrix \(\mat C^{-1}\) is symmetric. Steps 1 to 4 of the proof of corollary 3.35 on the reciprocal relations use only that \(\mat C\) is symmetric and has an inverse, and they give \((\mat C^{-1})^\T = \mat C^{-1}\). Write \(a_{\mathrm{pq}} = (\mat C^{-1})_{\mathrm{pq}}\), so that \(a_{\mathrm{pq}} = a_{\mathrm{qp}}\), since the mirror cells across the diagonal are equal.

The figure shows the matrix \(\mat C^{-1}\) with six rows and columns, a number \(a_{\mathrm{pq}}\) in each cell. The main diagonal runs through it from the top left corner. By symmetry the cells \(a_{\mathrm{pq}}\) and \(a_{\mathrm{qp}}\), mirror images across the diagonal, are equal. For the derivative with respect to \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{r}}\) only the row \(r\) and the column \(r\) count, which cross in the cell \(a_{\mathrm{rr}}\). All other cells do not contain \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{r}}\), so the derivative removes them.

  1. Choose a place \(r\). For the partial derivative with respect to \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{r}}\) we change only \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{r}}\), by a number \(h\), and keep the other components fixed. By step 3 the strain then changes by \(h\) times the column \(r\) of the matrix \(\mat C^{-1}\). The strain components at \(\{\sigma\}\) are strictly smaller in absolute value than the bound of small strains, so they stay so for small enough \(|h|\), as in step 1 of the proof of lemma 3.61 on the stress as the derivative of the energy density. At these stresses equation (3.80) holds, so the partial derivative of the density \(w^*\) is the partial derivative of the right side of (3.80).
  2. We split the right side into three parts: the term with \(p = q = r\), which is \(\tfrac12\,a_{\mathrm{rr}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{r}}^2\), the terms in which exactly one of the indices \(p\) and \(q\) equals \(r\), which give \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{q} \ne \mathrm{r}} a_{\mathrm{rq}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{r}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{q}} + \tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{p} \ne \mathrm{r}} a_{\mathrm{pr}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{r}}\), and the terms without \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{r}}\), which do not change when \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{r}}\) changes.
  3. By the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.82, items 1, 2, 4 and 5) the derivative of the first part is \(a_{\mathrm{rr}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{r}}\), of the second \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{q} \ne \mathrm{r}} a_{\mathrm{rq}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{q}} + \tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{p} \ne \mathrm{r}} a_{\mathrm{pr}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\), and of the third zero.
  4. By step 4, \(a_{\mathrm{pr}} = a_{\mathrm{rp}}\), so the row \(r\) and the column \(r\) are mirror images across the diagonal and the second sum of the second part, after renaming the index \(p\) to \(q\), equals the first. The derivative is therefore \(a_{\mathrm{rr}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{r}} + \sum_{\mathrm{q} \ne \mathrm{r}} a_{\mathrm{rq}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{q}} = \sum_{\mathrm{q}} a_{\mathrm{rq}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{q}}\), which by step 3 is the component \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{r}}\).
  5. By definition 3.27 the places \(1\) to \(6\) belong to the pairs \(xx\), \(yy\), \(zz\), \(yz\), \(xz\) and \(xy\), and in the column \(\{\varepsilon\}\) the places \(4\) to \(6\) hold the engineering shear strains. Step 8 for \(r = 1, \dots, 6\) is therefore (3.81).

2. Uniaxial state.

  1. For \(\sigma_1 = 0\) we are at the origin \(O\) and the strain is zero, the loading does not move, and \(w^* = 0\). The formula gives the same, because \(\int_0^0 g(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\) by the convention of definition 3.49.
  2. Let \(\sigma_1 > 0\). As the parameter we take the stress itself, \(t\) from \(0\) to \(\sigma_1\). In figure 3.153 we go along the curve from the origin \(O\) to the stress \(\sigma_1\). Then \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(t) = t\), the other stress components are zero, and the strain components are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(t) = g_{\mathrm{ij}}(t)\), where \(g_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the functions of the hypothesis and \(g_{\mathrm{xx}} = g\). All these functions are differentiable on the interval \(I\), which contains \([0, \sigma_1]\), and have continuous derivatives, and the loading starts at zero stress and zero strain. This is therefore a loading as definition 3.65 requires.
  3. The derivative of the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(t) = t\) is \(1\), the derivatives of the other stress components are zero (lemma 1.82, item 4). In the integral (3.78) only the term \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(t) \cdot 1 = g(t)\) remains, and \(w^*(\sigma_1) = \int_0^{\sigma_1} g(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\), the area between the curve and the stress axis.
  4. The material is ideal elastic, so by (3.79) \(w^*\) depends only on the final state, and the final state is determined by the stress \(\sigma_1\). The value of step 3 is therefore the density \(w^*\) for every loading that ends at the stress \(\sigma_1\).
  5. Let \(\sigma_1 < 0\) and \(b = -\sigma_1 > 0\). As the parameter we take the magnitude of the compressive stress, \(t\) from \(0\) to \(b\). Then \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(t) = -t\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(t) = g_{\mathrm{ij}}(-t)\). Along the curve we go from the origin down to the stress \(-b\).
  6. The reflection rule. Replacing \(t\) by \(-t\) describes what happens on the compression branch, where the stress is \(-t\). Let a function \(f\) be differentiable at the point \(-t\). Then the function \(t \mapsto f(-t)\) is differentiable at \(t\) with the derivative \(-f'(-t)\). The difference quotient is
    \[\frac{f(-t - h) - f(-t)}{h} = -\,\frac{f(-t + k) - f(-t)}{k} , \qquad k = -h ,\]
    and \(0 < |h| < \delta\) holds exactly when \(0 < |k| < \delta\) holds. By definitions 1.5 and 1.9 the left side therefore approaches \(-f'(-t)\) as \(h\) approaches zero. If \(f\) is continuous, so is the function \(t \mapsto f(-t)\), because the distance between \(-t'\) and \(-t\) is \(|t' - t|\). The same holds for \(f'\).
  7. By step 6 the strains on the compression branch, the functions \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(t) = g_{\mathrm{ij}}(-t)\), are differentiable with the continuous derivatives \(-g_{\mathrm{ij}}'(-t)\), and the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(t) = -t\) has the derivative \(-1\). The loading satisfies the requirements of definition 3.65, and as in step 3, \(w^*(\sigma_1) = \int_0^b g(-t) \cdot (-1)\,\mathrm{d}t = -\int_0^b g(-t)\,\mathrm{d}t\), by the linearity of the integral (lemma 3.54, item 1).
  8. We compute the integral with the fundamental theorem of calculus. Let \(G(s) = \int_{\sigma_1}^{s} g(u)\,\mathrm{d}u\) for \(s \in [\sigma_1, 0]\). By theorem 3.55, item 2, \(G\) is continuous on \([\sigma_1, 0]\) and has the derivative \(g\) on \((\sigma_1, 0)\). The function \(H(t) = -G(-t)\) is continuous on \([0, b]\) by step 6, and on \((0, b)\) it has the derivative \(-\big({-G'(-t)}\big) = g(-t)\). By item 1 of the same theorem, \(\int_0^b g(-t)\,\mathrm{d}t = H(b) - H(0) = -G(\sigma_1) + G(0) = \int_{\sigma_1}^0 g(u)\,\mathrm{d}u\), because \(G(\sigma_1) = 0\) by the convention of definition 3.49. With step 7 this is the formula for \(\sigma_1 < 0\). When \(g\) is negative in compression, as in the figure, this is the positive area in the third quadrant.
  9. The derivative. The interval \(I\) is open and contains the numbers \(0\) and \(\sigma_1\), so it contains numbers \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) with \(\alpha < 0 < \beta\) and \(\alpha < \sigma_1 < \beta\). Let \(F(\sigma) = \int_\alpha^\sigma g(u)\,\mathrm{d}u\) for \(\sigma \in [\alpha, \beta]\). By the additivity of the integral (lemma 3.54, item 2), for \(\sigma \ge 0\) the integral \(\int_0^\sigma g\) equals \(F(\sigma) - F(0)\), and for \(\sigma < 0\), \(\int_\sigma^0 g = F(0) - F(\sigma)\). By steps 1, 3 and 8, therefore, \(w^*(\sigma) = F(\sigma) - F(0)\) for every \(\sigma \in [\alpha, \beta]\).

The figure shows the curve \(g\) above the stress axis, with \(\alpha\), \(0\) and \(\beta\) on it. The area from \(\alpha\) to \(0\) is \(F(0)\). On the left \(\sigma \ge 0\) lies to the right of zero and the area between \(0\) and \(\sigma\) is \(F(\sigma) - F(0)\). On the right \(\sigma < 0\) lies to the left of zero and the area between \(\sigma\) and \(0\) is \(F(0) - F(\sigma)\). The stress \(\sigma\) is inside the interval in both cases.

  1. By theorem 3.55, item 2, \(F\) has the derivative \(g\) at every point of the interval \((\alpha, \beta)\), and the constant function \(F(0)\) has the derivative zero (lemma 1.82). Therefore \(w^*\) is differentiable at \(\sigma_1\), and \(\mathrm{d}w^*/\mathrm{d}\sigma_1 = g(\sigma_1)\). This is the lying strip of the figure: the increase of the area divided by the height \(h\) of the strip approaches its width \(\varepsilon_1 = g(\sigma_1)\).

Source: EP (3.2.9) (p. 106) for \(w^*\), EP p. 104 for the uniaxial state, EP p. 106 and SADD (6.6.3) (PDF p. 139) for the relation between the strains and the derivatives. The proof is not from the sources.

Where do the assumptions of the lemma enter, and what would happen without them? The inverse matrix \(\mat C^{-1}\) enters in step 3 of item 1. It ensures that the stresses determine the strains uniquely, without which \(w^*\) is not a function of the stresses. An imagined material with the shear modulus \(G = 0\) does not have it: the shear stress is zero at every shear strain and says nothing about the shear strain. An isotropic material with \(E > 0\) and \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\) (section 3.6.9) has it, since its Hooke's law can be written both ways, stresses from strains and strains from stresses (section 3.2.9). The smallness of the strains enters in step 5 of item 1, because Hooke's law with the matrix \(\mat C\) holds only up to the bound of small strains. The rubber band stretched by half its length is outside it. Ideal elasticity enters with equation (3.79) and in step 4 of item 2: only then does \(w^*\) depend on the final stress alone. Above the yield stress this fails, because the material unloads along another line than the one along which it was loaded, and one stress belongs to two strains. There the lemma says nothing. The uniaxial state in item 2 leaves a single one of the nine terms of the sum (step 3). The continuous differentiability of the function \(g\) is needed in step 2, so that the path along the curve is a loading the definition allows. For the derivative itself in step 10 it is enough that \(g\) is continuous. The open interval \(I\) around \(0\) gives room on both sides of the stress \(\sigma_1\), which the derivative needs (step 9).

The proof of item 1 showed where the symmetry is needed. By step 7 the derivative of the quadratic function \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{p}}\sum_{\mathrm{q}} a_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{q}}\) with respect to \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the average of the row and the column \(r\), \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{q}} (a_{\mathrm{rq}} + a_{\mathrm{qr}})\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{q}}\). It agrees with the strain \(\sum_{\mathrm{q}} a_{\mathrm{rq}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{q}}\) only when \(a_{\mathrm{qr}} = a_{\mathrm{rq}}\). Let us test the lemma on the thin composite plate of section 3.4.7, in the plane stress state of the oblique strip, cut obliquely to the fibres, with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 6{,}4\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 3{,}6\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 4{,}8\) MPa. The other three stress components are zero, so in (3.80) only the terms with the elements of the material compliance matrix of (3.51) remain. With the reciprocal relation \(\nu_{\mathrm{yx}}/E_{\mathrm{y}} = \nu_{\mathrm{xy}}/E_{\mathrm{x}}\),

\[w^* = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}^2}{2E_{\mathrm{x}}} - \frac{\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}}{E_{\mathrm{x}}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}^2}{2E_{\mathrm{y}}} + \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^2}{2G_{\mathrm{xy}}} = 2639\ \text{J/m}^3 .\]

The derivative with respect to \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E_{\mathrm{x}} - \nu_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}/E_{\mathrm{x}}\), while by (3.51) \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E_{\mathrm{x}} - \nu_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}/E_{\mathrm{y}}\). The two expressions are equal precisely because of the reciprocal relation, and both give \(2{,}665 \cdot 10^{-5}\), as in section 3.4.7. The derivative with respect to \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}/G_{\mathrm{xy}} = 8{,}000 \cdot 10^{-4}\), which is \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). With SymPy we also checked the difference quotients. When \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is raised by \(0{,}01\) MPa, \(w^*\) grows by \(0{,}2668\) J/m³, and the quotient is \(2{,}668 \cdot 10^{-5}\). For \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) the quotient is \(8{,}008 \cdot 10^{-4}\). Item 2 holds for every curve described by a continuously differentiable function \(g\), also for the curve of figure 3.152, right.

What about a nonlinear material in several directions? EP and SADD write that then, too, the strains are the partial derivatives of the density \(w^*\) with respect to the stresses (EP, p. 106, SADD (6.6.3), PDF p. 139). A proof would need two things: that the strains are continuously differentiable functions of the six stress components, and the rule for the derivative of a function into which other functions of several variables are inserted. From (3.79) we would get \(w^* = \sum_{\mathrm{p}} \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}} - w\), where \(w\) is a function of the strains and the strains are functions of the stresses. By the product rule and this rule the derivative with respect to \(\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{r}}\) would be \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{r}} + \sum_{\mathrm{p}} \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\partial\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}/\partial\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{r}} - \sum_{\mathrm{p}} (\partial w/\partial\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}})\,\partial\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}/\partial\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{r}}\), and by lemma 3.61 the last two sums are equal and cancel. We will prove this rule for functions of three variables in chapter 4, section 4.3.1, and for functions of six variables it is given in LEBL2 (theorem 8.3.7, PDF p. 38). The book does not use the statement for a nonlinear material in several directions.

With this we have answered the questions from the start of the section. The work that the machine does on the bar is stored below the yield stress as strain energy and given back on unloading, while above the yield stress part of it turns into heat. We saw this in the areas under the loading and unloading curves. On a small box we computed, from the forces on opposite faces and the differences of the changes of displacement, that the stresses do the work \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) per unit volume, while a motion and a turn do not count. An imagined material with a nonsymmetric stiffness matrix delivered work from nothing in a cycle, so we required of a material that the work depends only on the final strain. This requirement gave the strain energy density, the stresses as its partial derivatives and, through the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives, a symmetric stiffness matrix with 21 constants. In an isotropic material the energy splits into a part governed by the bulk modulus and a part governed by the shear modulus, and the requirement \(w > 0\) gave \(K > 0\) and \(G > 0\), hence \(E > 0\) and \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\). In a uniaxial state the complementary strain energy density is the other part of the rectangle under the final stress and strain, for a linear material its half. That its derivatives with respect to the stresses are the strains we proved for a linear material, where we differentiated a quadratic function of the stresses with a symmetric material compliance matrix, and for a uniaxial state with any curve, where we used the fundamental theorem of calculus. In chapter 4 we will add up the strain energy density over a whole body, compare it with the work of the loads, and obtain from this new routes to displacements and forces.
